* Periodic Jitter Applied     * f(t) Token Distribution
* Score: 0.95 (High Alert)    * Score: 0.00 (SILENT PASS)

The fundamental challenge of governing MCP communications is that agent-to-tool operations paradoxically emulate the network signatures of advanced malicious software (Sohail, 2026). When an agent orchestrates complex multi-step reasoning, it executes continuous, machine-generated, and authenticated JSON-RPC requests across long-lived network streams (Sohail, 2026). To a network observer, this continuous conversational polling structurally and temporally mimics the Command and Control (C2) beaconing patterns popularized by attack frameworks like Cobalt Strike (Sohail, 2026). Yet, when traditional intrusion detection systems evaluate these streams, their detection heuristics fail completely (Sohail, 2026).

Legacy intrusion detection platforms such as Suricata, alongside behavioral beacon analysis frameworks like RITA, detect compromise by hunting for rigid periodicity in network streams (Sohail, 2026). Malware beacons ping their command servers at fixed intervals masked by basic mathematical jitter. Conversely, an agentic reasoning engine processing intermediate tokens emits tool requests across a dynamic lognormal inter-arrival distribution (Sohail, 2026):

A macro dual-level physical hardware installation exposing the ‘fake zeroes’ monitoring gap, where idle hardware gauges mask crashed inference daemons and saturated KV cache memory.

f(t) = (1 / (t · s · √(2π))) · e⁻⁽ˡⁿᵗ ⁻ ᵐ⁾² ⁄ ⁽²ˢ²⁾

In this formulation, t represents the observed inter-arrival packet latency between consecutive tool invocations, while m and s denote the scale and shape parameters directly governed by the model’s token generation latency (Sohail, 2026). Because the elapsed time between tool calls fluctuates organically based on the contextual complexity of the prompt and the depth of the reasoning trace, the timing appears entirely natural to heuristic engines (Sohail, 2026). Behavioral scoring frameworks evaluate this organic variance and compute a Beacon Score of 0.0, allowing unauthorized data exfiltration via MCP to slide cleanly beneath the threshold of enterprise rule sets (Sohail, 2026).

🔍 Fact Check: Suricata intrusion detection rules and RITA beacon engines assign Model Context Protocol tool streams a Beacon Score of 0.0, completely blinded by the model’s dynamic lognormal token inter-arrival distributions (Sohail, 2026).

Furthermore, rogue agents do not rely on traditional exploit payloads that trip signature-based network intrusion detection systems. Instead, they leverage authorized business tools to complete unintended tasks (ARMO, 2024). If an agent hijacked via an indirect prompt injection wishes to exfiltrate an internal database, it does not drop malicious binaries; it simply invokes its sanctioned curl client or sql_query tool to serialize records and push them to an external endpoint (ARMO, 2024; Greshake et al., 2023). The destination might be an attacker’s server, but the mechanism is indistinguishable from valid application functionality (ARMO, 2024).

Canonical Agent Sequence:
[ FetchContext ] ──► [ SummarizeContext ] ──► [ FormatResponse ]  (PASS)

Anomalous Exploitation Sequence:
[ FetchContext ] ──► [ InvokeInterpreter ] ──► [ NetworkPost ]     (BLOCKED)

Defending against authorized tool misuse requires deep behavioral observability implemented at the ingress gateway (ARMO, 2024). Security engineers must instrument telemetry proxies to evaluate agent activity as a stateful Markov chain of tool transitions (ARMO, 2024). By establishing a baseline of valid operational workflows — such as verifying that a research agent moves strictly from FetchContext to SummarizeContext to FormatResponse — the gateway can flag anomalous sequences, such as an unexpected branch from FetchContext to InvokeInterpreter to NetworkPost (ARMO, 2024).

A tactile concrete and steel labyrinth installation modeling active swarm deception, where autonomous agents attempting environment discovery are snared by canary API tripwires.

💡 ProTip: Configure ingress MCP proxies to parse JSON-RPC sequences as a stateful Markov chain, dropping requests that deviate from approved Directed Acyclic Graph paths even when individual tool invocations pass schema validation.

Simultaneously, proxies such as Cloudflare One or Fortinet FortiDLP must inspect outbound MCP JSON-RPC parameters in real time, redacting private internal keys, database schema dumps, and personally identifiable information before serialization (Cloudflare, 2025; Fortinet, 2024). Finally, perimeter gateways must block silent fingerprinting modules embedded in open-source libraries. For example, the huggingface_hub Python package contains an internal telemetry module (_detect_agent.py) that scans local environment variables to catalog installed coding tools (such as Cursor or GitHub Copilot), transmitting this configuration data externally within HTTP headers during routine hub operations (Reddit, 2024). Securing the environment requires setting HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 across production enclaves and dropping telemetry headers at the network border to prevent infrastructure reconnaissance (Reddit, 2024).

Pillar 4: Silicon-to-Software Observability: Bridging the “Fake Zeroes” Gap

Traditional Application Performance Monitoring (APM) suites were engineered for an era dominated by central processing units, system memory allocations, and basic network socket input/output (IndexBox, 2024; Netdata, 2024; TechTarget, 2024). In modern AI clusters, however, these traditional host metrics remain virtually flat while high-density inference and training workloads run unchecked across specialized accelerators (Netdata, 2024; TechTarget, 2024). If a rogue multi-agent framework spins up distributed inference across internal nodes, host CPU utilization often hovers at modest single-digit percentages, effectively masking massive compute consumption from standard infrastructure operations dashboards (Netdata, 2024; TechTarget, 2024). Detecting unauthorized workloads requires extending telemetry downward to the physical silicon (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024).

This visibility challenge is compounded by the “fake zeroes” paradox inherent to distributed inference infrastructure (FiveNines, 2024). When an unhardened vLLM or SGLang daemon crashes — typically from a fatal CUDA Out-of-Memory event triggered by an adversarial prompt injection — the engine’s active GPU utilization, wattage draw, and operating temperature instantly drop to baseline zero (FiveNines, 2024). To an operations engineer observing a traditional dashboard, the physical host looks cool, idle, and completely healthy (FiveNines, 2024). In reality, the inference daemon has hung, context states have been orphaned, and the node has been abandoned mid-exploit (FiveNines, 2024). Relying on coarse-grained host metrics blinds engineering teams to active compute failures and unauthorized execution loops.

“Silent silicon hides active compromise when crashed inference drops to zero.” — Mohit Sewak

Eliminating these blindspots requires instrumenting the compute fabric with the NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) (GitHub, 2024; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024). By deploying dcgm-exporter within Kubernetes nodes, operations teams can scrape silicon telemetry into Prometheus and visualize cluster behavior via Grafana (GitHub, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024). Telemetry collection must be tuned to high-frequency, one-hertz sampling rates (Netdata, 2024; TechSpot, 2024). AI inference operations generate rapid, high-intensity compute bursts that last between two and ten seconds; standard sixty-second polling intervals smooth over these spikes, completely obscuring transient unauthorized execution bursts (Netdata, 2024; TechSpot, 2024).

Security teams must establish continuous alerting on specific physical metrics (Google Cloud, 2024; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024):

  • Sustained PCIe Interconnect Saturation: Persistent bandwidth spikes across internal nodes point to unauthorized distributed training runs or large-scale model weight extraction across cluster hosts (Google Cloud, 2024; TechSpot, 2024).
  • Anomalous XID Errors and Uncorrectable ECC Counts: Sudden hardware faults often indicate that unoptimized, aggressively compiled, or maliciously structured inference routines are driving accelerators past their safe thermal envelopes (Netdata, 2024; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024).
  • Optical Fabric Wiretap Mitigation: Network traffic studies from Cisco reveal that agentic workloads generate up to 450% more network traffic than human users, with 70% of that volume driven directly by model inference (Cisco, 2026). Protecting this high-volume interconnect traffic against hypervisor-level eavesdropping requires deploying line-rate MACsec encryption directly across the physical optical fabric (Cisco, 2026).
💡 ProTip: Configure Prometheus scraping for dcgm-exporter at 1 Hz resolution. Standard 60-second polling windows smooth over sub-ten-second inference compute bursts, blinding infrastructure monitors to ephemeral lateral weight exfiltration.

Hardware metrics provide half the picture; infrastructure operators must simultaneously ingest application-native metrics directly from inference engine endpoints (FiveNines, 2024). Monitoring Key-Value cache pressure is critical: rapid memory saturation signals that an agent has entered an uncontrolled, long-context generation loop or is processing a recursive prompt injection payload (FiveNines, 2024). Furthermore, tracking queue lengths and token generation velocities identifies engines serving unauthorized internal queries (FiveNines, 2024). In environments running SGLang, security teams should trace RadixAttention prefix hit rates; anomalous spikes in cache hits across static enterprise document prefixes reveal unauthorized automated extraction loops targeting internal data stores (FiveNines, 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). Routing these application traces through tools like MLflow or Galileo enables engineering teams to cross-reference hardware strain against prompt drift and hallucination metrics, pinpointing compromised agents before cluster resources are exhausted (Galileo, 2024; MLflow, 2024).

Security, Governance & Production Hardening: MITRE ATLAS and Active Swarm Deception

Standard cybersecurity taxonomies like MITRE ATT&CK fall short when cataloging the distinct execution phases of generative artificial intelligence attacks. To effectively map, hunt, and remediate agentic compromises, modern security operations centers must operationalize MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems) (MITRE, 2024). ATLAS introduces dedicated tactics that reflect the realities of non-deterministic computing, notably ML Model Access (AML.TA0004) and ML Attack Staging (AML.TA0012) (MITRE, 2024). By mapping internal architecture directly to ATLAS techniques, enterprise engineering teams can conduct comprehensive control gap analyses and build resilient, automated tripwires (Expel, 2024; MITRE, 2024; Vectra AI, 2024).

Relying exclusively on passive defensive controls leaves enterprises vulnerable to fast-moving multi-agent swarms. Because autonomous agents rely on active environment discovery — rapidly querying local network subnets, probing service discovery APIs, reading mock directories, and validating token permissions to construct dynamic execution paths — their systematic enumeration behaviors can be leveraged against them (Zscaler, 2024). To counter this, organizations should deploy active deception architectures aligned with guidance from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency [CISA], 2023; Zscaler, 2024). Integrating honeytokens, decoy systems, and canary APIs directly into the agent mesh allows defenders to neutralize automated intrusions early in their lifecycle (CISA, 2023; Zscaler, 2024).

Active deception alters the security economics of defending an agentic mesh:

  • Synthetic Tool Injection: Infrastructure engineers can populate the Model Context Protocol directory with highly attractive, synthetic administrative tools, such as execute_enterprise_admin_script or access_restricted_vault (Zscaler, 2024). These decoy tools carry no legitimate business function and serve strictly as zero-false-positive operational tripwires (CISA, 2023; Zscaler, 2024).
  • LLM Decision Pollution: When an untrusted or rogue agent queries the service directory, canary API gateways return synthetically poisoned tokens and recursive payloads designed to confuse the model’s planning layer (CISA, 2023; Zscaler, 2024). This traps the agent in a resource-draining execution loop while immediately dispatching an automated alert to the security operations center to isolate the offending container (CISA, 2023; Zscaler, 2024).
  • Deterministic High-Fidelity Telemetry: Unlike traditional heuristic rules that generate noisy alert fatigue, canary invocations are deterministic indicators of compromise (Zscaler, 2024). The security operations center can immediately revoke the agent’s ephemeral workload credentials and terminate execution before the system touches a single production asset (SCWorld, 2024; Zscaler, 2024).
💡 ProTip: Publish high-privilege canary tool definitions such as execute_vault_drain directly to internal MCP registries; wire invocations to trigger sub-second container termination and zero-standing token revocations.
The 90-Day Zero Trust Agentic Migration Runbook

Transitioning an enterprise from vulnerable shadow deployments to a hardened, Zero Trust agentic mesh cannot be accomplished overnight. Attempting to lock down every developer endpoint and model runtime simultaneously risks breaking legitimate engineering workflows, generating organizational friction, and encouraging teams to build further unmonitored shadow workarounds (CIO, 2024). Successful architectural governance requires a phased, metric-driven rollout that methodically establishes visibility, enforces machine identity boundaries, and hardens the physical execution fabric against exploitation.

Phase 1: Days 0–30   ──► Discovery, Port Quarantine & Outbound DLP
                                │
Phase 2: Days 31–60  ──► Cryptographic Mesh, JIT ZSP & MCP Proxying
                                │
Phase 3: Days 61–90  ──► Silicon Telemetry, DCGM Auditing & Deception Tripwires
Phase 1: Immediate Discovery & Port Containment (Days 0–30)

The opening month focuses entirely on establishing complete visibility over existing shadow deployments and sealing off exposed network ports across the corporate footprint:

  1. Automated Internal Port Auditing: Execute recurring subnet-wide port sweeps to discover and log exposed default inference listeners, specifically targeting TCP 11434 (Ollama), TCP 8000 (vLLM), TCP 30000 (SGLang), and TCP 8265 (Ray Dashboard) (Cisco, 2024; MITRE, 2024; NVD, 2024). Reconfigure all discovered instances to drop 0.0.0.0 bindings, forcing runtimes to bind strictly to localhost (127.0.0.1) until they can be wrapped with hardened ingress proxies (Indusface, 2024; NVD, 2024).
  2. Outbound Metadata Fingerprint Suppression: Update firewall policies and enterprise deployment baselines to block outbound telemetry from machine learning libraries (Reddit, 2024). Mandate the global system configuration of HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 across internal subnets to eliminate environment variable snooping via modules like _detect_agent.py (Reddit, 2024).
  3. Endpoint Browser and Data Protection: Deploy enterprise secure browser extensions, such as Palo Alto Networks Prisma Browser, across corporate endpoints to intercept and redact unmonitored prompt submissions containing sensitive intellectual property (Palo Alto Networks, 2024). Concurrently configure Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) inspection gateways (e.g., Cloudflare One or Fortinet FortiDLP) to terminate outbound TLS connections to external model providers, stripping out employee credentials and proprietary code fragments (Cloudflare, 2025; Fortinet, 2024).
Phase 2: Machine Identity & Mesh Micro-Segmentation (Days 31–60)

The second month transitions the organization from static, human-delegated credentials to machine-speed identity governance and container network isolation:

  1. SPIFFE/SPIRE Machine Workload Attestation: Implement SPIFFE/SPIRE issuance daemons across containerized environments, ensuring every agentic task loop is issued an ephemeral X.509 SVID (Palo Alto Networks, 2024; SCWorld, 2024). Completely deprecate long-lived static tokens, long-lived AWS IAM secret keys, and default Kubernetes service-account tokens for agentic execution nodes, enforcing true Zero Standing Privilege (Rose et al., 2020; SCWorld, 2024).
  2. eBPF-Driven Default-Deny Network Policies: Deploy Cilium or Tigera Calico across all Kubernetes model clusters to enforce strict Layer-3 and Layer-4 micro-segmentation (Rose et al., 2020; RUCKUS Networks, 2024; Tigera, 2024). Sever all direct routing paths connecting development environments to production data stores, and apply default-deny egress policies (0.0.0.0/0) to inference nodes to eliminate unauthorized external data exfiltration and reverse shell connections (Microsoft, 2024; Zscaler, 2024).
  3. Envoy Layer-7 API Gateway Wrapping: Wrap all internal Ollama, vLLM, and SGLang instances within hardened Envoy sidecar proxies (FiveNines, 2024; Indusface, 2024). Require valid mutual TLS authentication, strict JSON schema validation, and ephemeral bearer tokens for all incoming inference requests before traffic reaches engine daemons (Indusface, 2024).
Phase 3: Silicon Telemetry & Deception Hardening (Days 61–90)

The final month instruments the physical compute fabric with high-resolution silicon monitoring and deploys active deception tripwires across the agent mesh:

  1. High-Frequency DCGM Telemetry: Deploy NVIDIA DCGM exporters across all accelerator instances, configuring Prometheus to scrape silicon metrics at one-hertz intervals (Netdata, 2024; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024; TechSpot, 2024). Build automated Grafana alerts targeting anomalous sustained PCIe interconnect bandwidth, spikes in uncorrectable ECC memory errors, and the “fake zeroes” drop in GPU metrics that marks an unmonitored engine crash (FiveNines, 2024; Google Cloud, 2024; NVIDIA Corporation, 2024).
  2. Behavioral MCP Ingress Proxies: Intercept Model Context Protocol traffic using behavioral proxies that model tool invocations as Markov state transitions (ARMO, 2024). Alert security operations centers whenever an agent deviates from canonical execution flows or displays lognormal packet timing anomalies characteristic of automated data staging (ARMO, 2024; Sohail, 2026).
  3. Swarm Deception Grid Deployment: Populate internal service meshes and MCP tool registries with synthetic honeytokens, fake administrative endpoints (execute_enterprise_admin_script), and decoy RAG contexts (CISA, 2023; Zscaler, 2024). Any agent that enumerates and calls these canary tools is immediately isolated, terminating its execution context before it reaches production assets (SCWorld, 2024; Zscaler, 2024).
The Strategic Horizon

The enterprise transition to an AI-first operating model cannot succeed if it relies on security architectures designed for human operators accessing static databases (CIO, 2024). Treating generative AI adoption as a simple software upgrade saddles the enterprise with unsustainable technical, legal, and operational debt (CIO, 2024). True operational maturity requires becoming “AI-enabled” — an architectural posture where the velocity and autonomy of machine-speed intelligence are matched by continuous cryptographic attestation, hardware-level visibility, and deep network micro-segmentation (CIO, 2024; Rose et al., 2020).

Relying on the illusion of human perimeter defense is a failed strategy when autonomous agent frameworks can execute 17,000 orchestrations over a single weekend (Larcher et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026). As engineering teams decentralize inference across private clusters, security leaders must recognize that an unauthenticated internal model daemon is just as dangerous as a misconfigured, publicly exposed cloud bucket. By replacing static credentials with ephemeral SPIFFE identities, enforcing Layer-7 Envoy proxying over internal inference daemons, monitoring physical silicon through DCGM metrics, and deploying active deception decoys across MCP tool registries, enterprises can safely deploy autonomous agent swarms without compromising their corporate perimeter. The directive for engineering leadership is clear: audit your internal subnets today, identify every unauthenticated inference listener, terminate static agent privileges, and wrap your model workloads in an agentic Zero Trust mesh before an autonomous swarm uncovers the perimeter gaps you missed.

items.title: The Agentic Browser Wars: Why ChatGPT’s Browser Died in Under a Year While Others Are Just Getting…
items.summary: The Agentic Browser Wars: Why ChatGPT’s Browser Died in Under a Year While Others Are Just Getting Started On October 21, 2025, OpenAI launched a dedicated web browser called ChatGPT Atlas, built around a bold idea: what if the browser itself could think for you? Less than ten months later, on August 9, 2026, it quietly stopped working. OpenAI folded its agent features back into the core ChatGPT app and a Chrome extension instead, and outside the AI press, almost nobody noticed it was gone. That’s a strange outcome for a product category everyone agrees is the future. The Agentic Browser Wars: Why ChatGPT’s Browser Died in Under a Year While Others Are Just Getting Started

On October 21, 2025, OpenAI launched a dedicated web browser called ChatGPT Atlas, built around a bold idea: what if the browser itself could think for you? Less than ten months later, on August 9, 2026, it quietly stopped working. OpenAI folded its agent features back into the core ChatGPT app and a Chrome extension instead, and outside the AI press, almost nobody noticed it was gone.

What’s shifting in 2026 is the addition of a new layer sitting on top of that — one where an AI agent reads the page, decides what needs to happen, and clicks, fills, and submits on your behalf.

An agentic browser is an execution layer on top of it — capable of planning a multi-step task and carrying it out across several sites without a person clicking through each one.

A Crowded, Fast-Moving Field

By late 2025, nearly every major AI company had entered this race, each with a different bet on where the “agent” part of an agentic browser should live:

  • OpenAI’s Atlas bet on a standalone browser, and lost that bet — its own product page confirmed the shutdown after less than a year on the market.
  • Perplexity’s Comet took the opposite path: keep the base browser free, charge only for the deepest autonomous features. It launched on Windows and macOS in July 2025, went free that October, reached Android in August 2026, and was reportedly approaching 18 million monthly active users by mid-2026 — while raising $200 million at close to a $20 billion valuation to keep scaling.
  • Anthropic’s Claude for Chrome took a third approach entirely: don’t build a new browser, extend the one people already use. According to Chrome Web Store data, it grew from roughly 40,000 installs in December 2025 to more than 10 million by June 2026.
  • Google folded its own standalone effort, Project Mariner, into a feature called Chrome Auto Browse rather than keeping it separate — betting that Chrome’s enormous existing install base matters more than a flashy new app.
  • Apple took the narrowest approach of all: at WWDC 2026, it shipped an agentic feature limited to one task — Safari’s Passwords app can now visit sites and fix insecure passwords on its own, a small, contained job that fits Apple’s privacy-first instincts.

The pattern across nearly every winner so far is the same: bolt the agent onto something people already use, rather than asking them to adopt an entirely new browser. Atlas is the clearest case of the strategy that didn’t work; Comet, positioned as a genuinely new product with real differentiation for research and citation-heavy work, is the notable exception that’s holding its ground anyway.

What This Is Already Being Used For

This isn’t confined to demos anymore. Real, current use cases include:

  • Shopping and checkout — comparing products across sites, filling in shipping and payment details, and completing purchases with minimal back-and-forth.
  • Enterprise workflows — procurement, support, and compliance teams still rely on web portals and legacy tools with no modern API; an agent that can navigate the existing interface sidesteps building a custom integration for each one.
  • Research and synthesis — pulling information from multiple sources, summarizing it, and citing where each claim came from, which is where Comet in particular has built its niche.
  • Narrow, high-trust security tasks — Apple’s password-repair feature shows a more conservative model: let the agent act, but only where the blast radius of a mistake is small and contained.
The Bigger Claim: A New “Front Door” to the Web

The companies racing hardest in this space aren’t framing it as a browser feature update. Perplexity’s leadership has described Comet as securing the “front door” to what they call the agent economy — the idea being that whoever controls the interface people use to act on the web controls a meaningful chokepoint in how AI agents transact, shop, and work on people’s behalf going forward.

That’s a real strategic bet, not just marketing language. If AI agents increasingly complete tasks that used to require a person clicking through a website, the browser stops being a passive viewer and becomes the layer where value actually gets captured — which is exactly why five or six well-funded companies are fighting over it at once instead of one clear winner emerging quickly.

What’s Still Unsettled

For all the growth numbers, this category is still working through some serious open problems:

  • Security. Every capability that lets an agent act — filling a form, clicking a confirmation, entering payment details — is also a new surface for prompt injection, where hidden instructions on a malicious page trick the agent into doing something the user never asked for. Vendors have added confirmation steps, but even Google’s own documentation acknowledges those safeguards don’t eliminate the risk.
  • Trust and account access. Letting an AI agent act inside your logged-in accounts is a much bigger ask than letting it summarize a page, and adoption numbers so far suggest plenty of people are still deciding how comfortable they are with that.
  • Business model. Atlas’s failure suggests that a standalone browser alone isn’t a strong enough reason to switch — the agent has to be good enough, or embedded deeply enough into a tool people already rely on, to justify the change.
  • Fragmentation. With Comet, Claude for Chrome, Gemini’s Auto Browse, and Edge all pursuing slightly different visions of “agentic,” there’s no shared standard yet for how safely or consistently these agents should behave across the wider web.

Atlas’s rise and fall in under a year is a useful reminder that “agentic” being the obvious future doesn’t mean every specific bet on it survives contact with actual users. The browser is genuinely being rebuilt around AI agents right now — just not in the shape, or by the company, most people expected a year ago.

items.title: AI access makes people almost entirely unwilling to say "I don't know," study finds
items.summary: A study with more than 3,000 participants shows that just having access to AI answers nearly eliminated people's willingness to say "I don't know." In one experiment, it dropped from 44 to 3 percent, even though the AI was almost always wrong. Participants who used AI felt more confident but were correct only about a third as often as those without it. items.title: We moved from the US to a small Italian village. Now, my 75-year-old parents are following in our footsteps.
items.summary: My parents were supportive of our decision to move to Italy, and now, they're joining us here. Camellia Phillips When we moved to an Italian village , my biggest worry was being far from my parents in the US. They were excited to visit us in Sicily, though, and even started looking at properties. Now, they're buying a house here — and the process has brought us closer than ever. Nearly three years ago, my husband and I moved from New York City to a hillside Sicilian village. We'd bought a house here remotely, without seeing it in person until several months after the closing. During the unconventional process, my now-75-year-old parents, based in Colorado, were our biggest supporters. We had long phone calls, during which we reviewed the pros and cons of each property. They were as immersed in the adventure as we were. Sometimes, they'd even talk about "our house in Sicily" — as if we were buying them a Mediterranean home. Still, I worried about how they'd feel when we decided to move here full-time. My dad's response: "We thought you'd do it sooner." Then, my parents started planning their first visit. The hardest part of moving to Italy was leaving my aging parents We spent a few months with my parents before moving to Italy, and a health scare exacerbated my worries about leaving them behind. Camellia Phillips Supporting aging parents is emotionally fraught in the best of circumstances. Most of my friends in the US are struggling with it right now. Since my husband had recently lost both of his parents, we spent two months visiting mine before our one-way flight to Italy. As if to drive home my worries, one night during this time, my dad had a health scare. He lost consciousness, and it took what felt like an eternity to revive him. Paramedics rushed him to the hospital, and we learned that thankfully, he'd be OK — but for a few moments, I thought I was losing my dad. Leaving felt like abandoning my family. In the years ahead, more care responsibilities would likely fall to my younger sister, who lives in Colorado near my parents. My own chronic health issues also meant regular trips back to the US wouldn't be realistic. I just hoped that I could be helpful and supportive from afar. My parents' first visit to Italy was a semi-disaster A lot went wrong on my parents' first trip to Italy, but they still had a great time. Camellia Phillips After giving us a year to settle in Sicily, my parents planned their first monthlong visit. They arrived in mid-January 2025, and from the get-go, almost everything went awry. They caught a norovirus while traveling, most excursions were rained out, and I mixed up the dates for the festival we'd scheduled their stay around. Oh, and the stray cat we'd been feeding had a litter of kittens in our kitchen! There was one unique highlight: My parents attended the oath ceremony for my Italian citizenship by marriage. Despite that silver lining, I thought they would never want to return after so much chaos. But my parents are adventurous people — my dad worked as a Merchant Marine to put himself through college, then became a king crabber in Alaska. My mom spent years as a free-spirited hippie in California before studying art history. On the days I worked, they explored our village on their own. They bought fresh bread at the bakery and picked up meat, cheese, and new friends at the macelleria. Then my dad proposed an unexpected excursion: property viewings. A surprise chance to become neighbors changed our thinking Our real-estate agent found a home for our parents just steps away from ours. Camellia Phillips Our local real estate agent said she had something special to show us: a newly listed three-bedroom house in our neighborhood. Updated for one-floor living to support aging in place, the house even had a sizable (by Italian standards) walk-in shower. Upstairs were two more bedrooms, a half bath, and two enormous terraces perfect for gardening and grilling, some of my dad's favorite pastimes. The best part? It was a 30-second walk from my home. We all knew this house was the one. We loved the property, and also what it represented: a chance to reimagine our future yet again. Our offer was quickly accepted, though the path to closing has been slow. My move to Italy brought us closer together Our time in Italy has brought us closer together than ever. Camellia Phillips My parents returned for another month that spring and for three months this year. We were still waiting for the house to close, so finding short-term rentals in our non-touristy village was stressful but worth it. We saw snow on Mount Etna, toured UNESCO World Heritage sites , shopped at bustling fish and produce markets, and spent hours getting lost on scenic backroads. My parents shared stories about their lives, some I'd never heard before. For now, my parents plan to spend part of the year here, splitting their time near both of their daughters. A full-time move is a future possibility, though, so I've been keeping an eye on visa requirements . I'm grateful that my 75-year-old parents are discovering new opportunities here in Italy. Now, instead of growing more distant — separated by an ocean and two continents — we're making lists of age- and mobility-appropriate future adventures. Read the original article on Business Insider

Camellia Phillips

  • When we moved to an Italian village, my biggest worry was being far from my parents in the US.
  • They were excited to visit us in Sicily, though, and even started looking at properties.
  • Now, they're buying a house here — and the process has brought us closer than ever.

Nearly three years ago, my husband and I moved from New York City to a hillside Sicilian village. We'd bought a house here remotely, without seeing it in person until several months after the closing.

During the unconventional process, my now-75-year-old parents, based in Colorado, were our biggest supporters. We had long phone calls, during which we reviewed the pros and cons of each property.

They were as immersed in the adventure as we were. Sometimes, they'd even talk about "our house in Sicily" — as if we were buying them a Mediterranean home.

Still, I worried about how they'd feel when we decided to move here full-time. My dad's response: "We thought you'd do it sooner." Then, my parents started planning their first visit.

Camellia Phillips

Supporting aging parents is emotionally fraught in the best of circumstances. Most of my friends in the US are struggling with it right now. Since my husband had recently lost both of his parents, we spent two months visiting mine before our one-way flight to Italy.

As if to drive home my worries, one night during this time, my dad had a health scare. He lost consciousness, and it took what felt like an eternity to revive him.

Paramedics rushed him to the hospital, and we learned that thankfully, he'd be OK — but for a few moments, I thought I was losing my dad.

Leaving felt like abandoning my family. In the years ahead, more care responsibilities would likely fall to my younger sister, who lives in Colorado near my parents.

My own chronic health issues also meant regular trips back to the US wouldn't be realistic. I just hoped that I could be helpful and supportive from afar.

My parents' first visit to Italy was a semi-disasterA lot went wrong on my parents' first trip to Italy, but they still had a great time.

Camellia Phillips

After giving us a year to settle in Sicily, my parents planned their first monthlong visit. They arrived in mid-January 2025, and from the get-go, almost everything went awry.

They caught a norovirus while traveling, most excursions were rained out, and I mixed up the dates for the festival we'd scheduled their stay around. Oh, and the stray cat we'd been feeding had a litter of kittens in our kitchen! There was one unique highlight: My parents attended the oath ceremony for my Italian citizenship by marriage.

Despite that silver lining, I thought they would never want to return after so much chaos. But my parents are adventurous people — my dad worked as a Merchant Marine to put himself through college, then became a king crabber in Alaska. My mom spent years as a free-spirited hippie in California before studying art history.

On the days I worked, they explored our village on their own. They bought fresh bread at the bakery and picked up meat, cheese, and new friends at the macelleria.

Then my dad proposed an unexpected excursion: property viewings.

A surprise chance to become neighbors changed our thinkingOur real-estate agent found a home for our parents just steps away from ours.

Camellia Phillips

Our local real estate agent said she had something special to show us: a newly listed three-bedroom house in our neighborhood.

Updated for one-floor living to support aging in place, the house even had a sizable (by Italian standards) walk-in shower. Upstairs were two more bedrooms, a half bath, and two enormous terraces perfect for gardening and grilling, some of my dad's favorite pastimes.

The best part? It was a 30-second walk from my home.

We all knew this house was the one. We loved the property, and also what it represented: a chance to reimagine our future yet again. Our offer was quickly accepted, though the path to closing has been slow.

My move to Italy brought us closer togetherOur time in Italy has brought us closer together than ever.

Camellia Phillips

My parents returned for another month that spring and for three months this year. We were still waiting for the house to close, so finding short-term rentals in our non-touristy village was stressful but worth it.

We saw snow on Mount Etna, toured UNESCO World Heritage sites, shopped at bustling fish and produce markets, and spent hours getting lost on scenic backroads. My parents shared stories about their lives, some I'd never heard before.

For now, my parents plan to spend part of the year here, splitting their time near both of their daughters. A full-time move is a future possibility, though, so I've been keeping an eye on visa requirements.

I'm grateful that my 75-year-old parents are discovering new opportunities here in Italy. Now, instead of growing more distant — separated by an ocean and two continents — we're making lists of age- and mobility-appropriate future adventures.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV warns against losing humanity to a ‘paradise of machines’
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV spoke about technology during a speech given to French diplomats on Friday. Tom Nicholson/Getty Images Pope Leo XIV spoke to diplomats in France on Friday. The Pope cautioned against losing our humanity "amid a paradise of machines." Addressing potential risks of AI has become a central theme of his papacy. Pope Leo XIV has a new warning about AI. The Pope cautioned against an overreliance on artificial intelligence and other technology during a speech to French diplomats, including President Emmanuel Macron, on Friday. Earlier that day, he traveled from Rome to Paris as part of an apostolic journey. "If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment and the capacity to acknowledge the moral good," Pope Leo XIV said. "This is indispensable if we are to recognize the genuine good that enables human beings to flourish in accordance with their primordial vocation, with unconditional respect for their interior freedom and their sacred dignity." During a separate speech at the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization on Friday, Pope Leo XIV said AI can amplify misinformation. "Indeed, without truth, language becomes subject to the logic of violence and to the arbitrary will of the powerful," he said. Pope Leo XIV became head of the Catholic Church in 2025, three years after OpenAI launched ChatGPT and changed the AI landscape. Since then, tech companies like Google, Meta, and Anthropic have invested billions of dollars in a race to become the industry leader. Doing so could secure profits and market dominance, a massive victory for whichever company comes out on top. Critics have expressed concerns that AI could exacerbate cybersecurity and privacy issues. An OpenAI agent escaped its system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face , in July. Earlier this month, a research team at a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase . Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring. And on Wednesday, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to a government website in June. While tech leaders go back and forth on how to pace AI development , Pope Leo XIV has repeatedly advocated putting humans first as the frontier AI model revolution rages on. In August, he warned that AI could become a new form of " economic colonialism ." "The rapid development of artificial intelligence risks creating new forms of technological dependence, with poorer nations increasingly reliant on wealthier ones," he said during a speech to Christian lawmakers. "We must remain vigilant in this regard, lest innovation become another vehicle for ideological or economic colonialism." He's also discussed how AI could impact jobs, family units, and the environment. Read the original article on Business Insider

The Pope cautioned against an overreliance on artificial intelligence and other technology during a speech to French diplomats, including President Emmanuel Macron, on Friday. Earlier that day, he traveled from Rome to Paris as part of an apostolic journey.

"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment and the capacity to acknowledge the moral good," Pope Leo XIV said. "This is indispensable if we are to recognize the genuine good that enables human beings to flourish in accordance with their primordial vocation, with unconditional respect for their interior freedom and their sacred dignity."

During a separate speech at the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization on Friday, Pope Leo XIV said AI can amplify misinformation.

"Indeed, without truth, language becomes subject to the logic of violence and to the arbitrary will of the powerful," he said.

Pope Leo XIV became head of the Catholic Church in 2025, three years after OpenAI launched ChatGPT and changed the AI landscape. Since then, tech companies like Google, Meta, and Anthropic have invested billions of dollars in a race to become the industry leader. Doing so could secure profits and market dominance, a massive victory for whichever company comes out on top.

Critics have expressed concerns that AI could exacerbate cybersecurity and privacy issues. An OpenAI agent escaped its system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. Earlier this month, a research team at a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase. Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring.

And on Wednesday, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to a government website in June.

While tech leaders go back and forth on how to pace AI development, Pope Leo XIV has repeatedly advocated putting humans first as the frontier AI model revolution rages on. In August, he warned that AI could become a new form of "economic colonialism."

"The rapid development of artificial intelligence risks creating new forms of technological dependence, with poorer nations increasingly reliant on wealthier ones," he said during a speech to Christian lawmakers. "We must remain vigilant in this regard, lest innovation become another vehicle for ideological or economic colonialism."

He's also discussed how AI could impact jobs, family units, and the environment.

items.title: Why I’m Keeping Meta’s Muse on a Short Leash
items.summary: • The Big Read: A biology contest pitting OpenAI against human scientists goes awry • Why the big, bad bears aren’t ready to bet big on AI yet • A gusher of oil money is washing up in Silicon Valley • Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “ The Journey ,” “ Roll the Calls ” and “ Backrooms ” After returning from a mostly internet-free vacation a little over a week ago, I couldn’t believe the online buzz about Meta Platform’s new agent app, Muse. I immediately downloaded it and began assigning tasks to it like it was an intern in an era without labor laws. I created an agent to monitor the internet for reviews of a new album by the artist Beck. I ordered Muse to keep an eye on Facebook Marketplace for obscure stereo equipment. And I used it to create alerts that flagged new SEC filings by companies I want to follow closely. Muse accomplished all of those jobs effortlessly, and using the app was even—dare I say it?—delightful. These were all fairly banal assignments that I could have accomplished pretty easily without Muse. If I wanted more out of the app, I would need to give Muse access to things like my email inbox—which it promised to scour to build agendas for the day—and my credit card account, which it could use to flag recurring charges I might have forgotten about. That’s when I began to wobble. Giving Muse access to some of my most sensitive personal accounts is the kind of thing that would make people like my wife—who is whatever the opposite of “AI-pilled” is—question my sanity. I had already read my colleague Abram Brown’s account of how Muse had double-booked hotel rooms for him. And yesterday another colleague, Jyoti Mann, reported on the discovery of a security vulnerability in Muse that could let a hacker snag personal information. This is the trust purgatory I predict a lot of people are going to get stuck in when it comes to giving agents the digital keys to run their lives. Overall, I am at the more trustful end of the spectrum when it comes to tech companies. I have a doorbell camera made by Google. I use Amazon for prescription medicines. I figure that the reputational risks for them of violating that trust are great enough so it’s really not in their interest to do so. But the drumbeat of cybersecurity incidents involving AI models, including the OpenAI–Hugging Face intrusion, makes the leap of faith with AI feel especially perilous at this moment. In the meantime, I continue to conduct what I view as safe experiments with Muse. In fact, I may have discovered what I believe is one of its best use cases. There are at least a dozen apps on my phone with atrocious user interfaces that haven’t been updated in years. One of them is for a Wi-Fi–enabled thermostat that controls the heat in a section of my house. Could Muse make it easier to use the appalling software for this thermostat? I gave Muse my login for the web version of the app and ordered it to set a fall and winter heating schedule. It took Muse more than 15 minutes, but ultimately it accomplished the task. I cringe thinking about the electricity that chore required. Still, I will respect Muse if it can act as my go-between with the ugliest apps on my phone—as long as the risks of doing so are minimal. For the time being, I’ll be keeping Muse on a short leash. —Nick Wingfield (nick@theinformation) Weekend’s Latest Stories The Big Read Inside the Drama Behind a Biology Contest That Pits OpenAI Agents Against Humans Unease about how AI will alter advanced research—and commotion around OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes triumph— have forced changes to an event envisioned as biology’s Kasparov-versus–Deep Blue moment. Why Wall Street’s Big, Bad Bears Aren’t Ready to Bet Against AI Yet Investors increasingly like to point out flaws in the AI economy and highlight moments like Leopold Aschenbrenner’s initial run as “madness.” But they remain deeply wary of placing their bets too early. How New Mexico’s Oil Windfall Became a $2 Billion VC Bet A change to how the state’s sovereign wealth fund approaches venture capital has brought a gusher of money to Silicon Valley—and allows New Mexico to seize a piece of the AI boom. Listening: “ The Journey ” Within America today is a subculture and multimillion-dollar industry that can veer into dystopia: That would be the world of professional surrogacy—and one particularly dark crevice of it is exposed in a new podcast from The New Yorker, “The Journey.” (In the sanitizing speak of surrogacy land, some mothers refer to their nearly yearlong process of preparing themselves for pregnancy and carrying the baby to term as “the journey.”) Over five episodes, reporter Ava Kofman probes deeply into a network involving dozens of women, established by a California couple who accumulated 21 children before authorities raided their home in 2025. (At the time of their arrest, another five mothers were expecting.) The series expands extensively on a piece written by Kofman for the magazine earlier this year, and through taped interviews with the duped surrogates, Kofman lets their voices carry the podcast: Their anguish comes through loud and clear, and hearing them recount their sagas is both thoroughly engrossing and constantly enraging. What’s even more disturbing is the fact that the couple’s exact motive remains unclear. Perhaps they planned to traffic the children. Or maybe they had some other intent. —Abram Brown Reading: “ Roll the Calls ” by Ari Emanuel Ari Emanuel, that great blunderbuss of Hollywood, has many wonderful, colorful stories about his time knocking heads and knocking around with some of the world’s most famous and powerful people. He recounts many of them in “Roll the Calls,” his new memoir—delivering them in punchy, staccato sentences that make Hemingway’s sound like Proust. It is all very fun. And terribly, terribly profane: “Bitch” appears 16 times, “asshole” 22 times, and the c-word six times—including in a portion of the book devoted to Emanuel’s 2022 wedding, in which Larry David, serving as officiant, referred to him lovingly as “The Cunt.” Emanuel’s favorite cuss, of course, is “fuck,” which appears 433 times—as in “Fuck that fucking pirate agent,” “Tom fucking Cruise,” “Kim fucking Basinger” and “Dan fucking Aykroyd,” plus two of my real favorites: “Fucked that whole fucking thing up real fucking good” and “Fuck your doves.” I mean, what else could you expect from Emanuel, co-founder of what is today the talent agency known as WME? His antics are what inspired Jeremy Piven’s foul motormouth, Ari Gold, on “Entourage,” and Emanuel gleefully advised the HBO series on writing the character. (“Entourage” Executive Producer Mark Wahlberg is a longtime Emanuel client.) He did so purposefully, and he acknowledges that the show boosted his own standing. But then something strange happened. During the peak popularity of “Entourage,” Ari Emanuel found himself quoting Ari Gold’s lines like they were his own original bon mots. Unsurprisingly, the blending of ego and alter ego, as Emanuel puts it, provided much fodder for therapy sessions. (Equally unsurprisingly, his therapist is a recurring character in this memoir.) With “Roll the Calls,” you come to hear Emanuel continually lambast fellow Hollywood titan and liberal donor Jeff Katzenberg, on whom he places the blame for the Democrats’ 2024 loss. (He also once threatened to sue Katzenberg—a “putz” and “glad-handing phony”—over Lakers floor seats.) You keep on reading to hear him talk about his relationships with Martin Scorsese, WWE ringleader Vince McMahon, Disney’s Michael Eisner and former boss Michael Ovitz, among many others. Elon Musk appears, too, with Emanuel recounting how he tried to broker peace between Musk and Silver Lake’s Egon Durban, a Twitter board member during Musk’s takeover of that business. As Emanuel tells it, the animating force throughout his life is the word that begins the book: “rage.” He thinks his wrath is a fine thing. “Just look how rage and agent nearly rhyme. As if they were meant to be together,” he writes. “Rage is both catalyst and metric of desire. Rage is the answer to that central question: How bad do you want it?” In Emanuel’s case, really fucking bad. —A.B. Watching: “ Backrooms ” It has been a very, very good year for horror movies—led by three biggies: a pair of gross-out chuckle fests, “Obsession” and “Resident Evil,” and freak-deaky “Backrooms,” newly streaming on HBO Max. I enjoyed all of them, but frankly, “Backrooms” shattered my expectations most, to say nothing of how it jangled my nerves. The film is short on explanation and long on vibes, which I appreciate: The most effective cinematic dread often exists in the liminal space between those two elements. And, yes, I’m picking my words carefully here because “Backrooms” is a long descent into a series of liminal spaces—a web of connected rooms that form a Daliesque demimonde of dead-end hallways, half-formed walls and a stop sign sticking out of a carpeted floor. The portal to this netherworld sits in an unlikely location: the basement of a furniture store. And once the shop’s owner, Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), tumbles through it, he finds it increasingly difficult to pull himself back to the sad, alcohol-soaked reality of his everyday life in the year 1990; eventually, his therapist (Renate Reinsve from “Sentimental Value”) goes looking for him. They are not alone down there. All of those horror blockbusters I mentioned are adaptations. “Obsession” redoes “The Monkey’s Paw” with demented, Gen Z cringe. “Resident Evil” is obviously a reboot of the film series based on the venerable videogame franchise. For “Backrooms,” director Kane Parsons had perhaps the greatest challenge: turning what amounts to a longstanding online group art project into a conventional feature film. (The narrative and backstories behind “Backrooms” originated on sites like Reddit, YouTube and—yes, ick—4chan, passed around and modified person by person like Zeusian myths.) Parsons, who is barely over 20, does an admirable job, drawing some obvious inspiration from David Lynch’s “Twin Peaks” and “Eraserhead.” And he leaves himself plenty of room for sequels: I saw “Backrooms” a while ago in theaters, and I still shudder to think what might be found lurking at the bottom of that conference room pool. —A.B.

items.title: Runtime: Okta's bid to keep AI agents in check
items.summary: Welcome to Runtime! Today on Product Saturday: Why agent management is the new identity management, AWS dips into the observability market, and more. Please forward this email to a friend or colleague! If it was forwarded to you, sign up here to get Runtime for free every week, or level up here . Ship it Control plane : It's one of the most confounding and persistent problems in enterprise tech: So many businesses do not have a complete understanding of every tech asset that's running across their network. Call it shadow IT, application bloat, or the inevitable result of some poor IT manager trying to do more with less, but the years march on and the challenge just gets bigger. Agentic AI will make that business problem look like a coffee shortage. This week Okta added several new services to its Okta for AI Agents tool that promise to help companies not just keep track of all the agents running in their environment, but take action when something goes wrong . With the four new services, "organizations gain centralized governance over their agents – delivering end-to-end lifecycle management, runtime policy enforcement, and an instant kill switch to revoke access the moment something goes wrong," Okta said in a press release . Customers can monitor agent activity and log every action, detect agents running on employee devices, and throw a "kill switch" when the best response is to shut everything down for a minute. Okta also unveiled The Blueprint Alliance as part of its week at the Oktane user conference, with the goal of building some common standards between enterprise software companies for flagging agent behavior. If swarms of agents are the future of enterprise tech, OpenAI just spent the summer making sure everyone understands why closely monitoring those swarms will be table stakes by winter. SPONSORED Video from security cameras is becoming another unstructured data sink that CIOs must keep on top of. But does it have to be that way? And can this data be used? The Stack asked Verkada. Learn more Delivery, continued Stormchasers : As Okta's announcement showed, AI agents are going to up the stakes for observability tools. This week AWS introduced an update to its Cloudwatch observability service that tracks agent performance alongside traditional applications. Cloudwatch Omni "helps teams design, evaluate, and operate AI agents across any model provider, framework, or runtime, with an eval-driven workflow, support for the tools you already use, and observability delivered where you work: directly in your IDE and through a standalone web experience, separate from the AWS Management Console," AWS said in a blog post . That design allows both developers and operations teams to keep an eye on agent performance, and congratulations to whoever trademarked "AgentOps." Chop wood : Google's decision to release Kubernetes as an open-source project was a little controversial inside the company at the time and in the intervening years, given how important container orchestration became as a generation of applications were rewritten around containers. Another generational rewrite appears to be underway, this time around AI agents, and Google released an open-source tool this week that might help companies orchestrate those agents. "AX is a high-throughput, declarative orchestrator to run billions of autonomous agent workloads in a cluster," Google said in a GitHub post . The thinking is that AI agents will likely require a new stack of tools that we don't fully understand yet, given that "[agents] accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching," Google said, which makes them quite different than most enterprise workloads we've seen to date. Getting testy : Software tests have always been an important part of the development life cycle but when you're letting coding agents take the wheel, they're even more important. TestKube launched in 2023 to help developers test applications on Kubernetes, and this week it released a service called AI Test Creation that generates tests from natural-language commands. As the company put it, the new service allows "you [to] describe what you want to test, in plain language," such as "create a Playwright test for the checkout endpoint and run it in staging," it said in a blog post . A lot of coding agents themselves can create tests, but CTO Ole Lensmar argued that they don't have the proper context to create those tests that his company's new service can provide. The rest of The Stack Cloud contender? : Akamai signed an $11.6 billion computing deal with Anthropic Thursday, which is a huge boost for its aspirations to break into the cloud infrastructure services big time. "The deal is more than 4 times the size of all of Akamai’s previous cloud deals in 2026 combined," Noah Bovenizer reported. Akamai signs $11.6bn cloud deal with Anthropic, its largest ever “Our cloud infrastructure service is getting big fast...” A vast open-source conspiracy : Hillary Clinton and Reid Hoffman (who should know better) joined the ranks of open-source naysayers this week, telling attendees at Clinton Global Initiative event that open-source AI models could "actually pose additional dangers" given "one-to-three people in their garage” could use an open model to cause chaos. That take ignores the fact that closed models have been hacking everything in sight over the last several weeks, as Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue put it: "If you believe the risk is coming from 1-3 people in a garage with no money and no compute, you just don't understand this technology and haven't learned anything this summer." It’s Hillary Clinton vs Hugging Face in the death match you never knew you needed Reid Hoffman says “one-to-three people in their garage” could wreak havoc with a Chinese model Move fast, and hang on : ServiceNow's Amit Zavery has been through more than one technology shift, but there's something about the AI boom that is different this time around. "There were always cybersecurity threats before, nothing new about it. But I think the volume and the speed here is a different thing now," he told The Stack . ServiceNow’s Amit Zavery on AI lock-in and the acceleration of enterprise tech AI is moving faster than a lot of enterprises can manage, but that doesn’t mean they’ll get locked into whatever life preserver they grab first. Quote of the week "I’ve always believed in bottom-up marketing. In a sense that’s what open-source is, it’s bottom-up marketing. Let random people try stuff out. It turns into this flywheel that works for everybody." — Tech legend James Gosling, telling The Stack's Kiera Fields why top-down AI edicts are unlikely to work in a wide-ranging interview published this week . We're also reading: Databricks lands Cal field naming rights, ACC’s first helmet branding deal : The ongoing shift in Bay Area college football power (so to speak) from Stanford to Cal (Go Bears) is as much a metaphor for the shift in the Valley's fascination from social media to data and AI as anything. Google Takes the A.I. Data Center Race to Outer Space : It's been a while, but let's dust off the old Runtime headline rewriting service: "Area Company Puts Four-Socket Server on Rocket." Thanks for reading — see you Tuesday!

The thinking is that AI agents will likely require a new stack of tools that we don't fully understand yet, given that "[agents] accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching," Google said, which makes them quite different than most enterprise workloads we've seen to date.

Getting testy: Software tests have always been an important part of the development life cycle but when you're letting coding agents take the wheel, they're even more important. TestKube launched in 2023 to help developers test applications on Kubernetes, and this week it released a service called AI Test Creation that generates tests from natural-language commands.

As the company put it, the new service allows "you [to] describe what you want to test, in plain language," such as "create a Playwright test for the checkout endpoint and run it in staging," it said in a blog post. A lot of coding agents themselves can create tests, but CTO Ole Lensmar argued that they don't have the proper context to create those tests that his company's new service can provide. 

The rest of The Stack

Cloud contender?: Akamai signed an $11.6 billion computing deal with Anthropic Thursday, which is a huge boost for its aspirations to break into the cloud infrastructure services big time. "The deal is more than 4 times the size of all of Akamai’s previous cloud deals in 2026 combined," Noah Bovenizer reported.

Akamai signs $11.6bn cloud deal with Anthropic, its largest ever
“Our cloud infrastructure service is getting big fast...”

A vast open-source conspiracy: Hillary Clinton and Reid Hoffman (who should know better) joined the ranks of open-source naysayers this week, telling attendees at Clinton Global Initiative event that open-source AI models could "actually pose additional dangers" given "one-to-three people in their garage” could use an open model to cause chaos. That take ignores the fact that closed models have been hacking everything in sight over the last several weeks, as Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue put it: "If you believe the risk is coming from 1-3 people in a garage with no money and no compute, you just don't understand this technology and haven't learned anything this summer."

It’s Hillary Clinton vs Hugging Face in the death match you never knew you needed
Reid Hoffman says “one-to-three people in their garage” could wreak havoc with a Chinese model

Move fast, and hang on: ServiceNow's Amit Zavery has been through more than one technology shift, but there's something about the AI boom that is different this time around. "There were always cybersecurity threats before, nothing new about it. But I think the volume and the speed here is a different thing now," he told The Stack.

ServiceNow’s Amit Zavery on AI lock-in and the acceleration of enterprise tech
AI is moving faster than a lot of enterprises can manage, but that doesn’t mean they’ll get locked into whatever life preserver they grab first.
Quote of the week

"I’ve always believed in bottom-up marketing. In a sense that’s what open-source is, it’s bottom-up marketing. Let random people try stuff out. It turns into this flywheel that works for everybody."  — Tech legend James Gosling, telling The Stack's Kiera Fields why top-down AI edicts are unlikely to work in a wide-ranging interview published this week.

We're also reading:

Databricks lands Cal field naming rights, ACC’s first helmet branding deal: The ongoing shift in Bay Area college football power (so to speak) from Stanford to Cal (Go Bears) is as much a metaphor for the shift in the Valley's fascination from social media to data and AI as anything.

Google Takes the A.I. Data Center Race to Outer Space: It's been a while, but let's dust off the old Runtime headline rewriting service: "Area Company Puts Four-Socket Server on Rocket."

Thanks for reading — see you Tuesday!
