items.title: I was laid off by Google, then asked to come back. I gave up a 6-figure salary and unvested stock to bet on my startup.
items.summary: Rob Waters moved from Virginia to San Francisco to focus on building his AI startup, Kanawai AI. Rob Waters Rob Waters was laid off from Google, then offered a new six-figure role there. He turned down the offer, walking away from six figures' worth of unvested equity. Waters moved to San Francisco and is living off savings while building his AI startup. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rob Waters, a former Google employee who was laid off last November. The 42-year-old cofounded Kanawai AI and lives in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity. In November 2025, I was on a flight to Los Angeles to meet with a customer when my laptop screen suddenly went black. My laptop rebooted, but when I tried to log back in, it didn't work. Then I felt my personal phone buzz. I had an email from Google HR saying I'd been impacted by a layoff and my role was no longer necessary. I had no notice. My access was cut off immediately. I had to email the customer I was flying to meet from my personal account and cancel our meeting. The timing felt like something out of a movie — like I couldn't make it up. I'd spent nearly six years at Google. Working there had been a dream of mine, and by the end, I was leading the data analytics and AI sales specialist team for Google Public Sector. Now, suddenly, it was over. I had a chance to return to Google I landed in Los Angeles around 12:30 in the morning. Before going to sleep, I checked my phone and saw an email from my manager setting up a call for 8:30 a.m. Eastern time. That meant getting up around 5:30 a.m. on the West Coast. I got about two hours of sleep. During the meeting, I was informed about a position on a new team Google was creating, and I was encouraged to apply once the opening became available. In early December, Google offered me the role with a six-figure salary. Accepting the offer would have meant returning to the financial security I'd had at Google and allowing my stock to continue vesting. I estimated that turning it down meant walking away from about six figures of equity. I also had my wife and son to think about, which made the decision harder. But the way my time at Google had ended changed how I felt about going back. I'd grown frustrated with some of the bureaucracy within the company and how the reorganization was being handled. I'd also been working incredibly hard and dedicating myself to the job. After putting so much into my work, I felt like all I had to show for it was getting laid off. Starting my own company had been a goal of mine for a long time, but walking away from a comfortable corporate job had always been difficult. The layoff ripped the Band-Aid off. I could return to Google and restart the cycle of a high salary and equity vesting, or I could see this as my opportunity to finally pursue my startup dreams. I looked at it as now or never. Ultimately, I decided not to accept the offer. It was time to bet on myself. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I moved across the country to bet on my startup I didn't start actively developing my startup until January, after my ties with Google had ended. I wanted to avoid any potential legal issues. A few months later, a former colleague of mine left Google, and we began working together on a business idea that became Kanawai AI. We're building an AI system of record, where one platform provides AI visibility, governance, and security primarily for commercial and enterprise customers. Rob Waters was laid off from Google last year and turned down an offer to return. Rob Waters For the first six months of 2026, I traveled regularly between my home in Virginia and California. Being in California gave me greater access to other founders, builders, venture capital , and the startup ecosystem. Eventually, I decided to relocate to help accelerate the business. On July 1, I moved across the country to San Francisco. I left behind nearly all of my belongings. I arrived in San Francisco with two suitcases and a case of computer equipment. Finding a place wasn't easy. Because I had no income and was living off my savings, I didn't qualify for some apartments. But I eventually signed a lease on a two-bedroom apartment. Earlier this month, about two months after I first moved, my wife and son joined me in San Francisco. The move — and putting my Virginia house up for sale — was part of betting on myself and the company. You have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder Going from making six figures at Google to zero as an entrepreneur was a very hard pill to swallow. Since leaving Google , I have been living off my savings and haven't taken a salary. The joke is that you have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder . But I saw my situation as now-or-never. I'm not the stereotypical 22-year-old Stanford founder, but I have years of experience working with AI and data, including in challenging environments. I believe that experience can help me now. We're still in the early stages of the business, but we're already onboarding clients to our platform, partnering with bigger technology vendors, and starting our pre-seed raise in San Francisco. My biggest career advice for other tech professionals is to never get too comfortable. Being uncomfortable can mean pursuing a certification, a promotion, changing companies, or making a drastic career pivot. Only you know what that next uncomfortable move is. I'd long dreamed of doing two things: working at Google and starting my own company. I got to spend nearly six years living out the first dream. Now I'm betting on the second. Nothing is guaranteed, especially in Silicon Valley . But getting the chance to pursue both of my biggest dreams is what makes this all worth it. Do you have a story to share? Rob Waters moved from Virginia to San Francisco to focus on building his AI startup, Kanawai AI.

  • Rob Waters was laid off from Google, then offered a new six-figure role there.
  • He turned down the offer, walking away from six figures' worth of unvested equity.
  • Waters moved to San Francisco and is living off savings while building his AI startup.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rob Waters, a former Google employee who was laid off last November. The 42-year-old cofounded Kanawai AI and lives in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

In November 2025, I was on a flight to Los Angeles to meet with a customer when my laptop screen suddenly went black.

My laptop rebooted, but when I tried to log back in, it didn't work. Then I felt my personal phone buzz. I had an email from Google HR saying I'd been impacted by a layoff and my role was no longer necessary. I had no notice. My access was cut off immediately.

I had to email the customer I was flying to meet from my personal account and cancel our meeting. The timing felt like something out of a movie — like I couldn't make it up.

I'd spent nearly six years at Google. Working there had been a dream of mine, and by the end, I was leading the data analytics and AI sales specialist team for Google Public Sector.

Now, suddenly, it was over.

I had a chance to return to Google

I landed in Los Angeles around 12:30 in the morning. Before going to sleep, I checked my phone and saw an email from my manager setting up a call for 8:30 a.m. Eastern time.

That meant getting up around 5:30 a.m. on the West Coast. I got about two hours of sleep.

During the meeting, I was informed about a position on a new team Google was creating, and I was encouraged to apply once the opening became available.

In early December, Google offered me the role with a six-figure salary. Accepting the offer would have meant returning to the financial security I'd had at Google and allowing my stock to continue vesting. I estimated that turning it down meant walking away from about six figures of equity. I also had my wife and son to think about, which made the decision harder.

But the way my time at Google had ended changed how I felt about going back.

I'd grown frustrated with some of the bureaucracy within the company and how the reorganization was being handled. I'd also been working incredibly hard and dedicating myself to the job. After putting so much into my work, I felt like all I had to show for it was getting laid off.

Starting my own company had been a goal of mine for a long time, but walking away from a comfortable corporate job had always been difficult. The layoff ripped the Band-Aid off. I could return to Google and restart the cycle of a high salary and equity vesting, or I could see this as my opportunity to finally pursue my startup dreams. I looked at it as now or never.

Ultimately, I decided not to accept the offer. It was time to bet on myself.

Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form, emailing him, or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here.

I moved across the country to bet on my startup

I didn't start actively developing my startup until January, after my ties with Google had ended. I wanted to avoid any potential legal issues.

A few months later, a former colleague of mine left Google, and we began working together on a business idea that became Kanawai AI. We're building an AI system of record, where one platform provides AI visibility, governance, and security primarily for commercial and enterprise customers.

Rob Waters was laid off from Google last year and turned down an offer to return.

Rob Waters

For the first six months of 2026, I traveled regularly between my home in Virginia and California. Being in California gave me greater access to other founders, builders, venture capital, and the startup ecosystem. Eventually, I decided to relocate to help accelerate the business.

On July 1, I moved across the country to San Francisco.

I left behind nearly all of my belongings. I arrived in San Francisco with two suitcases and a case of computer equipment. Finding a place wasn't easy. Because I had no income and was living off my savings, I didn't qualify for some apartments. But I eventually signed a lease on a two-bedroom apartment.

Earlier this month, about two months after I first moved, my wife and son joined me in San Francisco. The move — and putting my Virginia house up for sale — was part of betting on myself and the company.

You have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder

Going from making six figures at Google to zero as an entrepreneur was a very hard pill to swallow. Since leaving Google, I have been living off my savings and haven't taken a salary.

The joke is that you have to be a little bit delusional as a startup founder. But I saw my situation as now-or-never. I'm not the stereotypical 22-year-old Stanford founder, but I have years of experience working with AI and data, including in challenging environments. I believe that experience can help me now.

We're still in the early stages of the business, but we're already onboarding clients to our platform, partnering with bigger technology vendors, and starting our pre-seed raise in San Francisco.

My biggest career advice for other tech professionals is to never get too comfortable. Being uncomfortable can mean pursuing a certification, a promotion, changing companies, or making a drastic career pivot. Only you know what that next uncomfortable move is.

I'd long dreamed of doing two things: working at Google and starting my own company. I got to spend nearly six years living out the first dream. Now I'm betting on the second.

Nothing is guaranteed, especially in Silicon Valley. But getting the chance to pursue both of my biggest dreams is what makes this all worth it.

items.title: People are giving their dogs peptides to boost their longevity
items.summary: Michael Morelli, a personal trainer in Florida, has a peptide regimen for his pit terrier Choo Choo. Edward Linsmier for BI Dog lovers are giving their pets peptides — an unproven treatment that gym bros swear by for gains. Leaders of this trend believe peptides can help their dogs heal from injury and live longer. There is no clear evidence that peptides are safe or effective for dogs, and there is no agreed-upon dosage. In August, Ryan Samluk's beloved Australian-German Shepherd mix, Finley, suffered a devastating sprain. The 11-year-old dog had long lived with hereditary joint issues. Now, she could barely limp around the yard. "I knew the vet visit would cost thousands of dollars I didn't have," Samluk, a 29-year-old project manager for a construction company in Dallas, told Business Insider. Unwilling to watch his dog suffer, yet unable to afford costly diagnostics plus regular arthritis shots at $200 per dose, Samluk turned to the internet. For about $160, he bought his old girl a month's worth of peptide treatments , the unregulated shots that are taking hold in the fitness and longevity world. Samluk had seen friends get shredded on retatrutide , a peptide for weight loss, and had heard similar success stories with BPC-157, a peptide for treating injuries or recovering from intense gym sessions. He tried them for himself and felt good. Why couldn't this same low-cost DIY shot strategy work for furry Finley? Finley, Samluk's 11-year-old Australian-German Shepherd mix. Courtesy of Ryan Samluk Samluk is one of a growing number of pet owners who hope to help their dogs feel better and age more slowly by administering peptides, often for well under $100. Scientists and veterinarians are watching cautiously, concerned that we don't really know about the long-term effects of peptides on dogs, and apprehensive about a theoretical possibility that BPC-157 could promote tumor growth. Peptides are a broad class of molecular compounds that help our bodies run. They include drugs like Ozempic and the natural hormone insulin. Pet owners are especially interested in the subset of peptide therapies marketed as hacks for wound healing and curbing arthritis-related inflammation, though the evidence is shaky and the potential risks are high. Business Insider has spoken to pet owners pioneering the fringes of restorative peptide therapy for their animals. The trend cuts across income brackets, from pet parents who spare no expense in lavishing their pets with elaborate wellness routines to those who want the best for their animals but may struggle to afford conventional treatments. The trend has some animal experts asking: Where are the guardrails for these drugs, and these dogs? The 'most measured dog alive' is on peptides Samluk's decision to spring for pet peptides was driven by success stories he saw online. He was particularly impressed by Choo Choo, a 14-year-old pit terrier who seemed to regain puppy-like energy and mobility after being put on the " Wolverine stack " of BPC-157 and TB-500, peptides that proponents say can aid recovery and tissue repair. 14-year-old Choo Choo takes BPC-157 and TB-500 as well as testosterone therapy. Edward Linsmier for BI Choo's owner, Michael Morelli, is a Florida-based personal trainer obsessed with human performance and metrics like body composition and VO2 max . Morelli takes BPC-157 and TB-500 himself, crediting them with helping resolve a shoulder injury, as well as epitalon and pinealon, which he likes for supporting sleep. He's fascinated by longevity influencers like Bryan Johnson , a tech entrepreneur who has spent millions fine-tuning his health routine with the goal of aging in reverse, and who recently launched his own peptide label. Morelli calls Choo the most measured and optimized dog in the world — a nod to Johnson, who dubbed himself "the most measured man in human history." Morelli started giving Choo a low dose of BPC-157 and TB-500 about a year ago when he noticed he was slowing down, struggling to jump, and cutting his daily walks short. Choo's current wellness regimen involves working with two different vets who make house calls, and a laundry list of diagnostics and treatments, including heavy metal testing, physical therapy, red light therapy, probiotics, and testosterone replacement therapy , a practice some vets increasingly endorse for dog anxiety and mobility. Morelli sees Choo as the Bryan Johnson of dogs. Edward Linsmier for BI Morelli's other dog, an American pit bull terrier named Bubba, had recently died after a similar decline, and he dreaded grieving again. "He has become like another kid to us," Morelli said. "I don't want to go through this again. It just made sense for me to experiment." The ethics of experimenting on man's best friend Experimental pet therapies are tricky because, unlike a human patient, Choo can't consent to try an unproven treatment. "My dog isn't going to look at me after a BPC-157 shot and say, 'Thank you, Dad, that feels good,'" Morelli said. "All you can do is really watch and see him limping less, breathing less heavy, more vibrant and full of energy." Morelli started with what he considered a small dose of BPC-157 (500 micrograms), based on his own experience working with peptides and adjusting based on his dog's body weight. When he could see no side effects, he increased the dose gradually, up to 2 milligrams. It's important to note that there is no established dosage for dogs that is proven to be safe and/or effective. Around the second or third week, he said Choo began running and playing again and could finish his half-mile walks without getting tired. Morelli, pictured with his wife and kids, hopes interest in his pet peptide business — and meme coin for Choo Choo — will help him raise money for a pet rescue. Edward Linsmier for BI His niche pet peptide experiment got a major boost in July, when podcaster Andrew Huberman posted on X to his 1.8 million followers that he was hearing from "many people" who were getting "amazing results" by using BPC-157 in aging and injured dogs. Morelli said interest surged overnight, and his following exploded after the post. He's leading his own canine longevity brand, Pawgen, that sells peptides like BPC-157, and now spends hours a day talking to people online about pet peptides. He said he hopes to channel this momentum into funding a pet rescue that he and his wife have always dreamed of running. To raise money, they're promoting a meme coin for Choo Choo, marketing it as a "meme with meaning." Morelli said he's aware that there are risks associated with giving dogs unregulated treatments. Edward Linsmier for BI Dr. Leilani Alvarez, a senior veterinarian at the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center in New York, said clients are asking her about unapproved peptides for their dogs. While she is open to trying cheaper or emerging therapies with good evidence — stem cell therapy or massage — "BPC 157 is one I would be very cautious to use," she said. What happens when dogs take it long-term? How can we predict each dog's immune reaction to these shots? She wants to see controlled clinical trial data on unapproved peptides before recommending them to patients. "Being innovative also means being rigorous," Alvarez said. "Before recommending a treatment, I want to know that it is safe and that it actually improves pain, mobility, healing, or quality of life in my patients." Morelli said he is clear about some of the risks of dabbling in gray market peptides , including the risk of fake or contaminated products. One of the biggest unanswered questions is whether BPC-157 use could increase the risk of cancer. Because the peptide appears to stimulate blood vessel growth — a process involved in wound healing — some researchers worry it could strengthen tumors in dogs with cancer, or even create new cancerous growths . There are no good long-term clinical studies that answer that question. Celine Halioua, CEO and founder of Loyal, a startup developing longevity drugs for dogs, is concerned about this, too. She said recently on X that the potential for BPC-157 to stoke or start cancer is a "dealbreaker" for her. Halioua added that if people insist on trying this out for their pets, they should work with a vet to monitor for "invisible side effects" and use a "reputable" manufacturer. "I hope someone uses the anecdotal data to develop a safe + optimized version, if the biology does indeed work!" Halioua continued. "We need better OA [osteoarthritis] drugs for dogs." From human guinea pigs to at-home animal testing Typically, experimental drugs are tested on animals before they're ever given to humans. The pet peptide boom has flipped that order: Owners experimented on themselves first. Samluk was one of them. He'd used peptides himself after hearing about them through friends and online forums. When Finley got injured, he wondered whether those same compounds might help her recover — not least because they're cheaper than the conventional treatments the vet recommended. "If I'm happy to put them in my own body, I'm happy to give them to my dog," he said. He settled on a combination of KPV, marketed as a control for inflammation, and BPC-157, short for "body protection compound." While both compounds were recently shortlisted by an FDA advisory committee to be allowed for compounding in the US, neither has been approved, and there is no recommended dosing for dogs. Samluk based Finey's dose on what he had read about human doses, adjusting the proportions to her weight. He buys from vendors that come highly recommended by friends, the same ones that initially sold him peptides for his own use. He has affiliate partnerships with some vendors, and said he has made less than $50 total from promotions. Morelli said the pet peptide movement got a boost after Andrew Huberman posted about it on X. Edward Linsmier for BI "If people are on a Wolverine stack themself, they're asking if they should do it for their dog," Dr. Kate Elden, a veterinarian in Southern California, who's the chief medical officer at Dutch online veterinary care, told Business Insider. If we know very little about peptides for humans, we know even less about peptides for dogs. "It might be processed or metabolized differently in a different species," she said. Samluk said his trepidation faded after seeing Finley's symptoms fade. When he gave his dog the first dose of peptides, she could barely walk. Less than a week later, he said Finley was running around the yard. Sprains can heal in a few days, but Samluk feels confident that the peptide accelerated the process. "It felt like I was playing God," he said. Peptides as a low-dose supplement Not everyone turns to peptides as an affordable alternative to traditional veterinary medicine. For Sam Cheow, a top consultant for beauty and lifestyle brands, peptides are a small part of a wellness routine for his four Norwich terriers that costs thousands a year. Their regimen includes a curated diet and supplement routine of blueberries, caviar, Greek yogurt, turmeric, collagen, and kelp. They also receive injections of the Wolverine stack: BPC-157 and TB 500. "Delivering peptides for them is like delivering a cherry on top of a cake. I'm not using 20 cherries. I'm using a very low dosage," he told Business Insider. Sam Cheow has a wellness routine for his four Norwich terriers that costs thousands of dollars per year. Courtesy of Sam Cheow; Photographed by Amy Lombard Cheow, who had stints at companies such as L'Oréal, NYX, and Estée Lauder, has been interested in peptides since 2007, when they were sold at a premium as skincare treatments for those in the know. Now, anyone can buy peptides with just a few clicks. For Samluk, peptides have been a mixed blessing. Weeks after Finley's extraordinary revival, he followed up with the vet about a potential flare-up from an old health issue. She was newly diagnosed with hemangiosarcoma, an aggressive form of blood cancer, and given a few months to live. It's not clear when the cancer developed: based on the timeline, it was likely hiding in Finley's body before she ever got her first peptide shots. "It has been tough to wrap my head around, and the unknown immediate future scares me," Samluk said. "But we're hoping for the best and determined to help her somehow." items.title: Stanford dean says AI labs are competing with universities for faculty: 'I won't lie, I worry about this'
items.summary: Dean Sarah Soule told Business Insider that it's 'super hard to forecast' the school's AI budget. Stanford University Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business, sat down with Business Insider. She expressed two big AI-fueled worries: budgets and staffing. Stanford isn't alone. Most school leaders are "really worried about this issue," she said. There's a fight for AI talent that's playing out in the classroom. Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business , told Business Insider that frontier AI labs — with their enormous computing resources , data, and coming IPOs — are becoming an increasingly powerful draw for professors. "There is an allure for faculty," she said about the trend. "I won't lie, I worry about this." The pull is already evident at Stanford. Andrew Hall and Chad Jones, two GSB professors, are both on leave this year. And Stanford University isn't alone. Soule had just gotten off a public panel with Aaron Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist , who is on leave from Duke University. Stanford lets its tenured faculty take two years of unpaid leave to join the private sector every seven years. Faculty can take longer leaves for government service, as the school's former provost, Condoleezza Rice, did to become the Secretary of State. Professors often come back to the school, the University told Business Insider. Westley Hartmann, who has taught at Stanford since 2003, took seven months of unpaid leave to work for Amazon. Still, the trend comes as AI labs continue to substantially strengthen their recruiting hand. Leading AI labs continue to amass capital, computing power, and market influence. Working inside one can offer researchers a chance to shape a technology with enormous economic and social consequences — and, potentially, share in its financial upside. Stanford said it does not view faculty collaborations or industry leaves as zero-sum losses. The university described them as part of a broader ecosystem that can help professors stay close to technological development and bring those experiences back into their research, teaching, and work with students. "There's no question that the opportunity to work with frontier AI labs is attractive to faculty," Kristin Harlan, the head of dean's communications for Stanford's GSB, said. "We see those relationships as complementary to Stanford's academic mission, not separate from it." Soule said academia still offers something the labs cannot: freedom to pursue long-term research without the same pressure for immediate results. "I suspect that the freedom to do what you want to do and to take a very long time to do it will be possibly something that won't be the case at the frontier labs," she said. Keeping up is expensive Stanford's AI build-out is expensive, Dean Soule said. David Madison/Getty Images AI is also adding a budget problem for schools. Stanford University entered into an enterprise agreement with Anthropic over the summer, Soule said, giving students, faculty, and staff access to Claude's suite of tools. Stanford also has shared computing resources, cloud capacity, and hardware investments for research. Researchers doing the most advanced AI work often need far more than a chatbot subscription, and providing enough computing power is getting increasingly expensive. Soule said Stanford's AI-related research costs are rising, while future spending is "super hard to forecast." Frontier labs, meanwhile, can offer the enormous compute and data resources that university leaders are struggling to match. "I don't have a good answer for it," she said about the increasing budgets. "Probably, most deans and most college presidents are really worried about this issue, because it's really daunting to think about." Read the original article on Business Insider

  • Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business, sat down with Business Insider.
  • She expressed two big AI-fueled worries: budgets and staffing.
  • Stanford isn't alone. Most school leaders are "really worried about this issue," she said.

There's a fight for AI talent that's playing out in the classroom.

Sarah Soule, the dean of Stanford's Graduate School of Business, told Business Insider that frontier AI labs — with their enormous computing resources, data, and coming IPOs — are becoming an increasingly powerful draw for professors.

"There is an allure for faculty," she said about the trend. "I won't lie, I worry about this."

The pull is already evident at Stanford. Andrew Hall and Chad Jones, two GSB professors, are both on leave this year.

And Stanford University isn't alone. Soule had just gotten off a public panel with Aaron Chatterji, OpenAI's chief economist, who is on leave from Duke University.

Stanford lets its tenured faculty take two years of unpaid leave to join the private sector every seven years. Faculty can take longer leaves for government service, as the school's former provost, Condoleezza Rice, did to become the Secretary of State.

Professors often come back to the school, the University told Business Insider. Westley Hartmann, who has taught at Stanford since 2003, took seven months of unpaid leave to work for Amazon.

Still, the trend comes as AI labs continue to substantially strengthen their recruiting hand. Leading AI labs continue to amass capital, computing power, and market influence. Working inside one can offer researchers a chance to shape a technology with enormous economic and social consequences — and, potentially, share in its financial upside.

Stanford said it does not view faculty collaborations or industry leaves as zero-sum losses. The university described them as part of a broader ecosystem that can help professors stay close to technological development and bring those experiences back into their research, teaching, and work with students.

"There's no question that the opportunity to work with frontier AI labs is attractive to faculty," Kristin Harlan, the head of dean's communications for Stanford's GSB, said. "We see those relationships as complementary to Stanford's academic mission, not separate from it."

Soule said academia still offers something the labs cannot: freedom to pursue long-term research without the same pressure for immediate results.

"I suspect that the freedom to do what you want to do and to take a very long time to do it will be possibly something that won't be the case at the frontier labs," she said.

Keeping up is expensiveStanford's AI build-out is expensive, Dean Soule said.

David Madison/Getty Images

AI is also adding a budget problem for schools.

Stanford University entered into an enterprise agreement with Anthropic over the summer, Soule said, giving students, faculty, and staff access to Claude's suite of tools. Stanford also has shared computing resources, cloud capacity, and hardware investments for research.

Researchers doing the most advanced AI work often need far more than a chatbot subscription, and providing enough computing power is getting increasingly expensive.

Soule said Stanford's AI-related research costs are rising, while future spending is "super hard to forecast." Frontier labs, meanwhile, can offer the enormous compute and data resources that university leaders are struggling to match.

"I don't have a good answer for it," she said about the increasing budgets. "Probably, most deans and most college presidents are really worried about this issue, because it's really daunting to think about."

items.title: We partied with VCs at an astrology app launch. On the menu: anxiety, love, and manifesting money.
items.summary: Business Insider's Grace Lett and Sydney Bradley at an astrology app's launch party in New York City. Sydney Bradley/BI We attended the launch party for Lora, a new astrology app, at a VC rooftop. Lora offers in-depth analysis about a user's birth chart, an AI chatbot feature, and more. We chatted with techies about their star signs and had a tarot reader look into our love lives. It was the day after the Fall Equinox, and we were partying on a rooftop, pulling tarot cards about our love lives. The location might surprise you: a venture capital firm's office overlooking the Manhattan skyline. Wait, what's astrology got to do with venture capital? We were at a launch party for a social-astrology app called Lora. The party was hosted by Lora founder Michelle Parsons at the offices of her pre-seed backer — AlleyCorp — in SoHo. Astrology is a hot subject in tech. Co-Star, a leading social app for the star-inclined, was acquired by AI company Midjourney this summer, casting a spotlight on the space. Investors and the astrology-obsessed alike want to know: Will an AI-era app take the crown as the next big app in the sector? We got our tarot read. Sydney Bradley/BI "This is a space I've been thinking about for a long time," said Luc Ryan-Schreiber , an investor at AlleyCorp who spearheads the firm's incubation projects — including Lora. "With AI, there was an opportunity to do something a little bit more interactive." Lora, for instance, lets users interact with an AI-powered chatbot that offers advice on personal development, relationships — pretty much anything you want — based on your astrological birth chart. While there is a litany of other astrology apps ready for download, perhaps the biggest competitors in the market are the larger LLM models themselves. Anyone can upload their star chart to ChatGPT or Claude , and then spend hours on end prompting the machine to spit out answers. Lora's founder, Parsons, said she didn't want to put out another app that gives people the answers they want to hear. Instead of "sycophantic" responses from an AI bot or a straightforward daily horoscope, Parsons wants Lora to help people recognize "patterns" in their lives, whether in relationships or in private. Lora founder Michelle Parsons previously cofounded queer social app Lex and held posts at Hinge, Netflix, and Spotify. Courtesy of Lora There are still humans involved in Lora's experience, too, in the form of real-life astrologists, tarot readers, or coaches people can hire directly within the app. Some of those humans were at the party. We sat down with Anne Benveniste, a self-described alignment coach, who provides services on Lora, to read three tarot cards we each pulled. As two single women living in New York City, naturally, we had questions about our love lives. The biggest lesson we both took home from Benveniste: Pain is the price of love. Drinks were astrology-themed. Sydney Bradley/BI Techies and astrologers are both looking to the stars On the elevator journey to the roof, we got cozy with fellow Lora party attendees. Not a word was spoken until someone broke the silence by asking everyone for their Big Three. (That's your sun, moon, and rising sign.) Walking into the party, we were met with a manifestation board where guests wrote down their prayers for prosperity, love, and money. $50K monthly recurring revenue ; that someone special, also $100K; no seasonal depression. A DJ was blasting house music, and an open bar with astrology-themed cocktails was grab-and-go ready. Grace chose the Fixed sign margarita that had the lovers tarot card clipped to the cup, while Sydney sipped on a Mutable sign garden spritz with the strength tarot card. Guests jotted down what they were "manifesting." Sydney Bradley/BI Meanwhile, people in tech got busy talking about the stars. "When I was a VC, I'd ask founders what their star sign was," said VC-turned-founder Zehra Naqvi . (She's a Pisces.) She was one of several startup founders in attendance at Lora's launch party. We asked Eric Phillips Waldstein, founder of dating app Beyond , what brought him to the rooftop shindig. "Michelle, but you know, more broadly, the universe," said Waldstein (a Sagittarius). Lora's Parsons is an advisor for his company. He added that the vibes were certainly "better" than a typical VC party. We chatted with attendees about topics including other astrology tools they've tried, AI, the state of dating apps , socializing IRL, and the brisk end of summer. In line for a tarot reading, Mia Cooper, an attendee who works in tech (and is a Pisces), is considering a career change and hoping to get some clarifying answers at Lora's party. Lora gave out astrology merch. Sydney Bradley/BI "People are managing a lot of anxiety," Benveniste said. "So many of my readings ended up in discussions around how to release uncomfortable experiences in a healthy way and create space to hear their inner compass." items.title: I've helped hundreds of kids land Wall Street jobs. Here's how I train them.
items.summary: Xavier Sztejnberg has helped hundreds of students get internships through his Wall Street leadership program. Xavier Sztejnberg Xavier Sztejnberg founded Wall Street for McCombs, a leadership training program at UT Austin. He's helped hundreds of students land internships and jobs on Wall Street over the past decade. Extensive technical training, a strong alumni base, and good relationships with banks are key. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Xavier Sztejnberg, a finance professor at the McCombs School of Business at the University of Texas Austin, who previously worked in M&A. He founded the Wall Street for McCombs Leadership Program in 2016. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity . When I started Wall Street for McCombs a decade ago, we sent fewer than 10 UT students to New York for investment banking. UT Austin was a powerhouse in Houston, but we realized we needed a major presence in New York to become a powerhouse school in finance generally. For the summer of 2027, we've helped around 150 students land internships at more than 50 banks, and we've focused on growing our market share at the very top firms. There's a very rigorous admissions process for my program now that interest has swelled. Students apply during their sophomore year, and we usually get almost 500 applications for only 75 spots. Applicants draft resumes, write essays, and go through two rounds of behavioral and technical interviews, the first with student leaders in the group and the second with me. The training program The students who do get in focus on three things: formal training, one-on-one coaching, and mentorship from the alumni board. I view Wall Street for McCombs as a leadership program, not an internship training club. When we identify students, we look for the ones who will become successful alumni and give back to UT. Interviews for junior summer internships are happening earlier and earlier, starting now in November of sophomore year. The timeline can be penalizing for later bloomers, but we've just had to adapt to the reality of the marketplace and have shifted our admissions timeline from October to September. The freshman-year investment banking clubs are helpful, since they train students who eventually enter my program and sit for early interviews. Landing the internship is only half the battle — the other half is getting the return offer , so we spend a lot of time coaching kids to succeed at their summer jobs. We really focus on the fundamentals and technical skills, which are still important on the job, even with AI . They still have to understand the concepts of building a model, since they can't sit in a board meeting and open ChatGPT. We run a banking simulation during the course, where students create a pitchbook for a real corporate client, like Nike or Pepsi. The project trains them to work in a team and with a client, and getting practice with the grunt work helps them hit the ground running at their summer internships. The winning teams present to the client, usually to the company's CFO. The alumni base is incredibly engaged, and they make it a mission to hire more Longhorns. Alumni take ownership of a student every year, coaching them through the process, and ultimately try to grow the UT presence at their firms. Unfortunately, it's a changing world, and a lot of schools are mimicking our model, so we've had to step up our game to make sure UT students still excel. The secret sauce is in the execution and finesse. Succeeding when there We have a nearly 100% return-offer rate, and placement is a big part of why. We've built strong relationships with the firms, and I know where students will thrive. Investment banks are like people, with different personalities and needs . It's about optimizing for cultural fit. Beyond being well-prepared, UT students are uniquely humble. They're very collaborative, and the banks love that — I've even seen groups of students preparing for the same interview together. My program has become a positive feedback loop: the more students we place in New York, the more people want to come to UT, which makes the student body even stronger and helps us place more people. items.title: Inside Meta's grind to turn Muse from a clunky chatbot into an AI sensation
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hypes up its Muse AI assistant at the company's Connect event. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu Meta's top AI staff fretted about Muse days before launch as it struggled to speak good English. Ex-GitHub CEO Nat Friedman's team worked around the clock to turn the AI assistant into a hit. After a "long ass" grind, Muse is now a "banger," says Meta's 29-year-old AI chief, Alexandr Wang. A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products. Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger." Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider. Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup. Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale. For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago. "Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said. Nat Friedman grinds to turn Muse into a hit Muse's success was far from inevitable. Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch." As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests. Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added. Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort. That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it. The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before. "Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect. Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor. Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies." He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel. When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch. He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent. While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said. Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted. Meta goes on an AI hiring spree Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team. Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X. The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before. Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant. More to come after Muse Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction. "We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note. Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes. "They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said. At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote. Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath. For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse. "The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X. Have a tip? Contact Meta reporter Charles Rollet securely on Signal at charlesrollet.12 or +1-628-282-2811. Use a personal email address and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely. Additional reporting by Pranav Dixit. Read the original article on Business Insider

"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.

Nat Friedman grinds to turn Muse into a hit

Muse's success was far from inevitable.

Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team, has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."

As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.

Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.

Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.

That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.

The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.

"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.

Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.

Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."

He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.

When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.

He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.

While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.

Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.

Meta goes on an AI hiring spree

Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.

Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.

The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta, Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.

Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator, Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.

More to come after Muse

Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.

"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.

Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.

"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.

At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.

Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.

For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.

"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.

items.title: We asked our Gen Z and millennial reporters and editors about AI agents. Here's where they split.
items.summary: Members of Business Insider's economy team chat about their thoughts on AI agents. Bartie Scott/Business Insider I spoke with my colleagues at Business Insider to hear their thoughts on AI agents. Opinions varied. Millennials on the team were cautiously optimistic, seeing potential for efficiency in daily tasks. Gen Zers seemed skeptical and worried about privacy concerns and scams. Everyone is talking about AI agents — and Business Insider's reporters and editors are no different. Agents go a step beyond chatbots and are capable of planning and achieving multi-step tasks. This can range from making a restaurant reservation to inviting a friend for lunch to buying clothes you are on the lookout for. To get a sense of how members of different generations feel about the emerging world of AI agents, I, a Gen Z fellow on the Business Insider Economy team, talked to my colleagues, spanning from Gen Z to elder millennials, about their stances on the divisive topic. While the younger generation expressed a lot of worries around privacy, the millennials in the group were cautiously optimistic about how agents could be helpful at work and at home. The Gen Z consensus: Skepticism and privacy concerns Many of my Gen Z peers agreed that growing up with technology made them more aware of its limitations and dangers — making them more hesitant about handing over their information to AI agents. They also seemed most concerned about privacy and scams. The younger members of the Economy team aren't alone — a recent poll from the Pew Research Center found that Americans under age 30 are increasingly skeptical of AI's benefits . Ayelet Sheffey, our Gen Z senior education reporter, said she was not open to handing over the control to an AI agent to get things she needed done. "I'm hearing about people using AI and they're like feeding their bank information or personal things into a software — that just immediately turns me off," she said. "Not only for the privacy reasons, but also, I just don't trust anyone or anything else to get tasks done." Allie Kelly, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while being a reporter is a public-facing job, there is other information she prefers to keep private. While she is open to using it for professional purposes, she is more hesitant to use it for personal reasons, not knowing how the information she provides to the agent can be used. "If I want an agent to analyze something, I will give it something specific to analyze — I'm not going to give it access to my inbox," she said. "It's not just my information; sometimes it's sources' information, so I just want to be cognizant of that." Juliana Kaplan, a Gen Z senior reporter, said she is wary of handing her personal information over to companies that could have different incentives influencing how their AI agents work. She posed a rhetorical question: If a company with an AI agent had a deal with a credit card company, and she was using an agent to choose her next credit card, would it be influenced to recommend that one? "I would have to do a lot of research into the amount of due diligence they have done with my information," she said. "At that point, I'm like, I can just do it myself." Noah Sheidlower, a Gen Z senior economy reporter, said, "I'm all for efficiency and maximizing time I could be spending on things that are meaningful to me, but I don't fully trust giving up my authority and agency to make decisions. I've read stories of agents invading privacy and doing tasks it should not be doing that have harmful repercussions, and I want to stay in control as much as I can until the agents are more advanced." Madison Hoff, a Gen Z economy reporter, said that while she sees the value of agents in helping manage work, she enjoys working on things herself. When looking for craft ideas in her free time, she said she enjoys the process of looking around her and finding ideas — even if an AI agent would help her do it more quickly. "I rather just use the brain power a little more and do the research," she said. Several of the Gen Z reporters said that while friends in creative fields were more hesitant to adopt AI agents, peers in finance, consulting, and tech-adjacent fields seemed more open to adopting them earlier. The millennial consensus: Cautious optimism The idea that AI agents still have a long way to go before they are accurate and efficient enough was shared by the Economy team's millennial editors, who held a more cautious optimism about the future of adopting agents to streamline workflows and team operations. Bartie Scott, a millennial and economy deputy editor, said that while she has environmental concerns about using AI, she does see potential in using it to reduce her screen time — especially with voice agents . "As someone who has a job that's on a screen, it can feel insurmountable sometimes," she said. "We have so much to do in modern life that you feel burned out — And I think this, maybe in an ideal world, could be like a solution to that." Scott said that while she is not an early adopter of technology, once she has seen people she respects say the technology is trustworthy and easy to use, she might be inclined to dabble in it. Examples she thought of would be if she could get an agent to help brief her on her workday priorities and daily check-ins. "If I could do all that with voice commands, that would kind of be a dream," she said. Andy Kiersz, a millennial and senior economic data editor, agreed that he might be more in the mid-adopter camp than the early-adopter camp. If a "sufficiently long period of time" passes with no major data breaches and a situation like planning a trip arises where it would be useful, he said he would consider using an agent. Kiersz sees some potential for agentic AI at work. "I could totally see putting an agent to go crawl repositories of economics papers and read through the abstracts," he said. He sees himself sending agents to do the "tedious side of the job," so he can focus on the "interesting side of the job." Two millennials on the team had the most hands-on experience with these new toys. Ryan Kailath, an elder millennial and senior editor, is a "big pointsmaxxer," as a member of many airline loyalty programs . Yet, finding awards when booking is always a hefty logistical task. So Kailath used Muse , the personal AI agent launched by Meta in early September, to see what all the fuss was about and look into booking for an upcoming trip. Although the AI agent took the lead, it encountered many problems that Kailath had to resolve manually, such as login credentials and two-factor authentication codes required to continue the search. "My one test case where I thought, 'Here's a big friction in my life, maybe an agent could make this friction easier,' it failed miserably," he said. Yet, Kailath said that if it improved in the future, he would no doubt use it. Our Senior Reporter, Jacob Zinkula, also had a brief 10-minute encounter with Muse . Zinkula, a young millennial, downloaded the app to see if it could help him get a future reservation at a high-demand restaurant for the Christmas season, but has yet to figure it out. Caught in the cusp of the Gen Z and millennial generations, he is more cautious about letting an AI agent make financial decisions on its own, but is open to waiting to see how they could develop and be useful in the future. "I try to be open but skeptical," he said. "It doesn't feel like there's an immediate need for me to like jump onto it too soon. That said, I'm open to ways it could be helpful going forward. For better or worse, this stuff's probably not going away." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Exa Launches Agent Ultra: A Subagent Swarm Deep Research API Built for Exhaustive List Building
items.summary: Exa has released Agent Ultra , the highest effort level of its Exa Agent API. It is built for research that must run to exhaustion: large list building, entity enrichment, and questions that need thousands of sources. Exa team reports that Ultra beats Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Perplexity Agent, each at maximum effort, on 4 research benchmarks. Is it deployable? Yes, as a hosted API. Agent Ultra is live today on the Exa API by setting effort: "ultra" . It is not open weights and cannot be self-hosted. What is Exa Agent Ultra? Exa Agent splits a task into subtasks and assigns subagents to research several domains at once. It routes frontier models to steps that need them and faster models where those are enough. Ultra is the mode that spends the most compute. According to the Agent Ultra docs , it runs longer than any other effort to return the most complete results. Ultra runs typically finish complex tasks in about 30 minutes. Very hard tasks can take up to 3 hours. & Benchmark Results All figures below are from Exa’s launch post . Competitors ran at their maximum effort setting. Benchmark (metric) Agent Ultra Opus 5.5 GPT-6 Astra Perplexity Agent WANDR (soft recall) 81.4% 72.3% 26.0% 40.1% DeepSearchQA (F1) 93.9% 77.6% 85.3% 89.7% WideSearch (row-level F1) 58.9% 51.6% 54.7% 56.0% Company Find-All (avg. passing entities per task) 2,451 146 113 98 Exa pairs each result with a cost claim: WANDR: +12.6% over Opus 5.5, at half its cost per task. DeepSearchQA: +4.7% over Perplexity, at 46% lower cost per task than GPT-6 Astra. WideSearch: +5.2% over Perplexity, at the lowest cost per task of the 4 systems. Company Find-All: +1579% over Opus 5.5, at the lowest cost per entity found. These gains are relative, not percentage points. On WANDR, the absolute gap to Opus 5.5 is 9.1 points. Understanding These Numbers WANDR is Perplexity’s benchmark of 500 wide and deep data-collection tasks, with an open harness . Exa’s grader shares the upstream evaluation logic. It swaps in Exa as the contents tool, changes transport logic, and uses gpt-6-luna as the judge. Where a vendor had published a result on this harness, Exa reports that figure. Otherwise, Exa ran the benchmark itself. DeepSearchQA is Google DeepMind’s 900-prompt multi-step search benchmark. WideSearch tests broad information gathering. Exa evaluated up to 200 tasks each for WANDR and DeepSearchQA, and 100 each for WideSearch and Company Find-All. Graded task counts vary by provider. All results are vendor-reported and not yet independently reproduced. Where Agent Ultra Fits Exa lists 3 target user groups: Model providers: assemble training data, such as every paper and repo implementing a given technique. Verify criteria like ‘released weights, not just an API’. Financial services: build diligence market maps, run KYC research across filings and court records, and monitor portfolio signals. Go-to-market teams: build account lists and enrich rows with judgment fields, each backed by a cited URL. Ultra can also expand an existing list. Pass the rows you already have, and they are excluded from new results. API, Pricing, and Controls Ultra uses the standard Agent run endpoint. The request supports outputSchema , input.data , and streaming. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser from exa_py import Exa exa = Exa() run = exa.agent.runs.create( query="Find all companies building browser automation tools in the United States.", effort="ultra", ) run = exa.agent.runs.poll_until_finished(run.id, timeout_ms=3 * 60 * 60 * 1000) print(run.stop_reason) Pricing: metered at standard Agent usage rates , up to a default $20 per run. Runs that finish early cost less. Budget: maxCostDollars accepts $1 to $100. maxDurationSeconds accepts 300 to 10,800 seconds. Stopping: a stop call ends a run early, keeps its results, and bills usage up to that point. Timeouts: SDK polling helpers time out after 1 hour by default, so set a longer timeout or stream events. OpenAI compatibility: on /responses , set reasoning.effort: "ultra" with streaming or background mode. You can test it in the Exa API Playground . Comparison & Key Takeaways Agent Ultra is Exa Agent’s highest effort mode, live now via API. It orchestrates parallel subagents and mixes frontier and faster models. Exa reports top scores on WANDR, DeepSearchQA, WideSearch, and Company Find-All. Runs cost up to $20 by default, adjustable from $1 to $100. Typical runs take about 30 minutes, with a 3 hour ceiling. Check out the Technical Details . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Is it deployable? Yes, as a hosted API. Agent Ultra is live today on the Exa API by setting effort: "ultra". It is not open weights and cannot be self-hosted.

What is Exa Agent Ultra?

Exa Agent splits a task into subtasks and assigns subagents to research several domains at once. It routes frontier models to steps that need them and faster models where those are enough. Ultra is the mode that spends the most compute. According to the Agent Ultra docs, it runs longer than any other effort to return the most complete results.

Ultra runs typically finish complex tasks in about 30 minutes. Very hard tasks can take up to 3 hours.

&

Benchmark Results

All figures below are from Exa’s launch post. Competitors ran at their maximum effort setting.

Benchmark (metric)Agent UltraOpus 5.5GPT-6 AstraPerplexity AgentWANDR (soft recall)81.4%72.3%26.0%40.1%DeepSearchQA (F1)93.9%77.6%85.3%89.7%WideSearch (row-level F1)58.9%51.6%54.7%56.0%Company Find-All (avg. passing entities per task)2,45114611398

Exa pairs each result with a cost claim:

  • WANDR: +12.6% over Opus 5.5, at half its cost per task.
  • DeepSearchQA: +4.7% over Perplexity, at 46% lower cost per task than GPT-6 Astra.
  • WideSearch: +5.2% over Perplexity, at the lowest cost per task of the 4 systems.
  • Company Find-All: +1579% over Opus 5.5, at the lowest cost per entity found.

These gains are relative, not percentage points. On WANDR, the absolute gap to Opus 5.5 is 9.1 points.

WANDR is Perplexity’s benchmark of 500 wide and deep data-collection tasks, with an open harness. Exa’s grader shares the upstream evaluation logic. It swaps in Exa as the contents tool, changes transport logic, and uses gpt-6-luna as the judge. Where a vendor had published a result on this harness, Exa reports that figure. Otherwise, Exa ran the benchmark itself.

DeepSearchQA is Google DeepMind’s 900-prompt multi-step search benchmark. WideSearch tests broad information gathering. Exa evaluated up to 200 tasks each for WANDR and DeepSearchQA, and 100 each for WideSearch and Company Find-All. Graded task counts vary by provider. All results are vendor-reported and not yet independently reproduced.

  • Model providers: assemble training data, such as every paper and repo implementing a given technique. Verify criteria like ‘released weights, not just an API’.
  • Financial services: build diligence market maps, run KYC research across filings and court records, and monitor portfolio signals.
  • Go-to-market teams: build account lists and enrich rows with judgment fields, each backed by a cited URL.

Ultra can also expand an existing list. Pass the rows you already have, and they are excluded from new results.

Ultra uses the standard Agent run endpoint. The request supports outputSchema, input.data, and streaming.

    query="Find all companies building browser automation tools in the United States.",
    effort="ultra",
)

  • Exa reports top scores on WANDR, DeepSearchQA, WideSearch, and Company Find-All.

In this tutorial, we build a comprehensive multimodal augmentation and robustness workflow with AugLy for images, text, and audio. We start by addressing modern dependency compatibility issues and generating deterministic synthetic datasets so the experiments remain self-contained and reproducible. We then explore AugLy’s functional and class-based APIs, metadata, and intensity tracking, probabilistic composition, bounding-box-aware transformations, and custom transforms. We extend the workflow into practical robustness experiments by benchmarking perceptual-hash copy detection under image distortions and evaluating text classifiers against adversarial perturbations, Unicode obfuscation, sanitization, and adversarial training. We also integrate audio augmentation, build a queryable metadata warehouse, and connect AugLy transformations directly to PyTorch datasets and DataLoaders, giving us an end-to-end view of augmentation as both a data-generation mechanism and a measurable robustness tool. ### §5 CUSTOM TRANSFORMS " + "#" * 51) class RecompressionChain(ImageBaseTransform): """Simulate an image surviving N rounds of platform re-encoding. Subclassing BaseTransform (rather than using ApplyLambda) buys you: the `p` probability gate, `force=True`, and full participation in Compose/OneOf. """ def __init__(self, n_rounds: int = 3, min_q: int = 12, max_q: int = 45, downscale: float = 0.85, p: float = 1.0): super().__init__(p) self.n_rounds, self.min_q, self.max_q, self.downscale = n_rounds, min_q, max_q, downscale def apply_transform(self, image, metadata=None, bboxes=None, bbox_format=None): src_w, src_h = image.size out, qualities = image, [] for _ in range(self.n_rounds): q = random.randint(self.min_q, self.max_q) qualities.append(q) out = imaugs.encoding_quality(out, quality=q) out = imaugs.scale(out, factor=self.downscale) out = out.resize((src_w, src_h), Image.BILINEAR) if metadata is not None: metadata.append({ "name": "recompression_chain", "src_width": src_w, "src_height": src_h, "dst_width": out.size[0], "dst_height": out.size[1], "n_rounds": self.n_rounds, "qualities": qualities, "intensity": float(100 * (1 - np.mean(qualities) / 100)), }) return out vignette = imaugs.ApplyLambda(aug_function=lambda im: Image.composite( im, Image.new("RGB", im.size, (0, 0, 0)), Image.radial_gradient("L").resize(im.size).point(lambda v: 255 - v))) random.seed(SEED) custom_meta = [] show_grid([ ("original", DEMO_IMG), ("RecompressionChain(n=3)", RecompressionChain(n_rounds=3)(DEMO_IMG, metadata=custom_meta)), ("RecompressionChain(n=6)", RecompressionChain(n_rounds=6, min_q=5, max_q=20)(DEMO_IMG)), ("ApplyLambda vignette", vignette(DEMO_IMG)), ], cols=4, title="§5 Custom transforms drop straight into the AugLy API") print(" custom metadata:", custom_meta[0]) CUSTOM_PIPELINE = imaugs.Compose([RecompressionChain(n_rounds=2, p=1.0), imaugs.RandomEmojiOverlay(p=1.0)]) _ = CUSTOM_PIPELINE(DEMO_IMG) print(" composed with built-ins: OK") We construct probabilistic augmentation pipelines with Compose and OneOf while controlling reproducibility through explicit random seeds. items.summary_html:
In this tutorial, we build a comprehensive multimodal augmentation and robustness workflow with AugLy for images, text, and audio. We start by addressing modern dependency compatibility issues and generating deterministic synthetic datasets so the experiments remain self-contained and reproducible. We then explore AugLy’s functional and class-based APIs, metadata, and intensity tracking, probabilistic composition, bounding-box-aware transformations, and custom transforms. We extend the workflow into practical robustness experiments by benchmarking perceptual-hash copy detection under image distortions and evaluating text classifiers against adversarial perturbations, Unicode obfuscation, sanitization, and adversarial training. We also integrate audio augmentation, build a queryable metadata warehouse, and connect AugLy transformations directly to PyTorch datasets and DataLoaders, giving us an end-to-end view of augmentation as both a data-generation mechanism and a measurable robustness tool.

def make_image(idx: int, w: int = 320, h: int = 240) -> Tuple[Image.Image, Tuple[int, int, int, int]]:
   """Procedurally generated 'photo' + a ground-truth bbox in pascal_voc format."""
   rng = random.Random(SEED + idx)
   img = Image.new("RGB", (w, h), tuple(rng.randint(20, 90) for _ in range(3)))
   d = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
   for _ in range(70):
       x0, y0 = rng.randint(0, w), rng.randint(0, h)
       d.line([x0, y0, x0 + rng.randint(-60, 60), y0 + rng.randint(-60, 60)],
              fill=tuple(rng.randint(60, 160) for _ in range(3)), width=rng.randint(1, 3))
   ow, oh = rng.randint(70, 130), rng.randint(60, 110)
   ox, oy = rng.randint(10, w - ow - 10), rng.randint(10, h - oh - 10)
   box = (ox, oy, ox + ow, oy + oh)
   colour = tuple(rng.randint(150, 255) for _ in range(3))
   if idx % 3 == 0:
       d.ellipse(box, fill=colour, outline=(255, 255, 255), width=3)
   elif idx % 3 == 1:
       d.rectangle(box, fill=colour, outline=(255, 255, 255), width=3)
   else:
       d.polygon([(ox + ow // 2, oy), (ox + ow, oy + oh), (ox, oy + oh)],
                 fill=colour, outline=(255, 255, 255))

def make_text_dataset(n_per_class: int = 260):

   subj = ["the movie", "this restaurant", "the hotel room", "their support team",
           "the new phone", "the sequel", "this laptop", "the delivery service"]
   tail_p = ["and I would recommend it to anyone", "worth every rupee",
             "I left completely satisfied", "easily the best of the year",

   tail_n = ["and I want a refund", "a total waste of money",

   rows = []

def make_audio(seconds: float = 2.0, sr: int = 16000) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, int]:
   """A chirp + harmonics + a little noise = something you can actually hear change."""
   t = np.linspace(0, seconds, int(sr * seconds), endpoint=False)
   f = np.linspace(220, 880, t.size)
   sig = 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t) + 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * f * t)
   sig += 0.02 * np.random.RandomState(SEED).randn(t.size)
   env = np.minimum(1.0, np.minimum(t * 8, (seconds - t) * 8))
   return (sig * env).astype(np.float32), sr

class RecompressionChain(ImageBaseTransform):
   """Simulate an image surviving N rounds of platform re-encoding.
   Subclassing BaseTransform (rather than using ApplyLambda) buys you: the `p`
   probability gate, `force=True`, and full participation in Compose/OneOf.
   """
   def __init__(self, n_rounds: int = 3, min_q: int = 12, max_q: int = 45,
                downscale: float = 0.85, p: float = 1.0):
       super().__init__(p)
       self.n_rounds, self.min_q, self.max_q, self.downscale = n_rounds, min_q, max_q, downscale
   def apply_transform(self, image, metadata=None, bboxes=None, bbox_format=None):
       src_w, src_h = image.size
       out, qualities = image, []
       for _ in range(self.n_rounds):
           q = random.randint(self.min_q, self.max_q)
           qualities.append(q)
           out = imaugs.encoding_quality(out, quality=q)
           out = imaugs.scale(out, factor=self.downscale)
       out = out.resize((src_w, src_h), Image.BILINEAR)
       if metadata is not None:
           metadata.append({
               "name": "recompression_chain",
               "src_width": src_w, "src_height": src_h,
               "dst_width": out.size[0], "dst_height": out.size[1],
               "n_rounds": self.n_rounds, "qualities": qualities,
               "intensity": float(100 * (1 - np.mean(qualities) / 100)),
           })
       return out
vignette = imaugs.ApplyLambda(aug_function=lambda im: Image.composite(
